GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GRAND MASTER
In reviewing the I 09th Annual Communication. so ably and skillfully
presided over by the Grand Master, we must come to the conclusion that
either providence controls our affairs so that we had a perfect presiding
officer, or we must conclude that we have an abundance of talent among
our elective officers, and perhaps the logical conclusion is that it is a
combination of both.
Certainly, Most Worshipful Leo E . Anderson, Grand Master. pre~
sided over and conducted the affairs of the dedicatory Communication in
a manner which brought great credit to the Grand Lodge of California.
The distinguished Masonic dignitaries. from all over the world, were loud
in their praise of the dignity with which the ceremonies were conducted
and the masterful manner in which the business sessions were conducted.
Combined with a perfect knowledge of Grand Lodge procedure and an
understanding of the issues which were before the Grand Lodge, Brother
Anderson accorded every brother the opportunity to discuss the issues
and yet, without cutting off deba te. kept to schedule and the harmony of
the Craft was preserved.
The biographic facts concerning Brother Anderson will appear at the
close of this brief tribute to him, and they will reveal the many and varied
activities which have commanded his time and interest. They will not.
however, reveal many things about the man. They will not, for example,
reveal the happy married life which he has had through the years with
Hollis ("Holly") . Nor will they indicate the great joy which both of
them have in their daughter, Denise, and their son. David. Neither will
they show the happy hours which they have had riding together, nor
the week~ends of pleasure around the pool at their beautiful home. The
sketch will state that Brother Anderson served as president of the San
Gabriel Country Club, but it will not also s how that he is an excellent
golfer, never so much so as when the chips are down and a difficult shot
must be made or a long putt holed to win a match or a wager.
Every Grand Master leaves the office having made many, many
friends throughout the jurisdiction, and certainly this is true of Brother
Anderson. He has thousands of friends among the Lodges, but the more
important truth is that, because of his geniality, his friendship and his
constant willingness to serve them and the Craft, he will keep these
friends throughout his lifetime. His name will rank high in the list of
Grand Masters who have performed outstanding service to this Grand
Lodge.

LEO E. ANDERSON
Grand Master

September 27, 1957 -

October 3. 1958

"LOOK AHEAD ..
DR. J. WHITCOMB BROUGHER, GRAND CHAPLAI N

Most Worshipful and Members of Grand Lodge:
I want to express my appreciation to Leo Anderson and to all of the
officers of the Grand Lodge for the joy that has been mine serving as
Chaplain this past year. It has been a wonderful year for me. I ha ve
made so many new friends. and found so much inspiration in all of our
activities, and my heart is most grate ful.
Most of you know that Leo has been my friend for nearly fort y years.
We were in college together, and the friendship has continued through
life. It was my privilege to tie the knot when he was married.
When they were married. Leo and Hollis did not wish to have too
much notice made of the fact that they were just married . when on their
honeymoon, so they agreed to keep it a secret. When they got on the
train Leo tipped the porter five dollars and said. "We are just married
and we want some real service , but we don't want anybody else to know
that we are just married. so please keep it quiet and tell no one ." E verything went alons:i all right until the next morning when they w ere walking down through the Pullman ca rs to the dining room , and Hollis said ,
"Look at the people staring at us. Somebody must have told them that we
are just married.'. After breakfast Leo got the porter aside and said .
"Didn't I ask you to say nothing about the fact that we are newlyweds?"
The porter said. "Yes. suh. boss." Leo said. "Folks looked at us like they
knew we are just married. Did you tell anybody?" He said, "No suh,
boss ! I didn't tell anybody.'' Leo said. " Well. it looks like they know.
Did anybody ask you?" He said. "Yes suh. One of dem old ladies asked
me if you were just married. and I said, No. dey ain't just married, dey 's
just good friends!"
Last year when I was here at Grand Lodge to be installed as Chaplain we went back on the train after Leo had become Grand M aster.
When Leo was ready to get off the train the porter brushed him off
vigorously and said, "I hope you had a good trip. Judge." Leo said , "I
had a good trip. but I'm not a judge.'' The porter sa·id. "Pardon me,
governor." Then Leo said, "Nor am I the governor." Then the porter
said. "What am you, anyway?" And Leo said. "I am the Grand Master
of the Grand Lodge of California." The porter brushed him off vigorously and said, " I knowed you was a face card when I saw you in the
first place!"
I want to express my appreciation to all of the men who have been
in the various meetings where I have had the privilege of saying a word ,
and telling a joke or two. You have all been very kind to my jokes, except
in one place where we had a banquet. After I had talked for a few
minutes, one stood in the back of the room, walked quietly up to the

11

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

front of the room, and as he passed the speakers stand he whispered, in
a stage whisper, "Your jokes are terrible!" I looked at the men alon~
the table to see if I could get some indication from them as to what it
was all about. The man went back to his seat, and about five minutes
later he got up again, walked up forward, and as he passed the microphone he whispered again, "You are talking too long!" I .thought s_omebody was pulling a joke on me, and I looked for some kmd of a tip-off
from the head table, but no one gave me any clue. The man went back
and sat down. and in about five minutes he got up again and came up
past the head table and said, "We all wis h we were home!" So I turned
to the chairman and said, "Who is that man?" And the chairman said,
"Don't pay any attention to him. He doesn't have an original idea in his
head. He just says what he hears other folks saying around him!"

You w ill find there are three kinds of people who look ahead. Those
that I call super-optimists. I like the spirit of optimism. It sees the bright
side of life. It sees the good in others. The spirit of optimism is what
makes a teakettle sing when it is up to its neck in hot water! But a superoptimist is a man who says everything is going to be all right. You don't
need to work for it. plan for it, or do anything about it. Sit down, take it
easy, eat, drink. and be mer ry. and let tomorrow take care of itself ...
super-optimistic about the future.
Then there are those who are pessimists. They look ahead and believe everything is going to be bad, they can remember everything bad
that has ever happened before, and tell you it is going to happen again.
The pessimist has no confidence in himself. or in his fellow men, or in
God. He lacks confidence so much that he wears both suspenders and a
beit!
A pessimist never wants to do a nything about the future because he
says nothing can be done. If you try it will be worse. He is like the man
who swallows an egg whole, and then is afraid to move for fear he will
break it, and afraid to sit still for fear it will hatch! No matter what he
does, something bad is going to happen. That is the pessimist. A pessimist and a super-optimist sit down together and do nothing.
This young king was neither a super-optimist nor a pessimist. God
had made him an offer. He looked ahead to see what he wanted.
Firs t, he looked at his father. David, who had been king. Read the
record. It says, "Thou hast blessed my father according as he walked
r ighteously before Thee." It is a good thing to learn the lessons from the
past. In our work in the Grand Lodge it is helpful for us to know what
has happened so we can include the good things and leave out the notso-good things in our future plans. In your Blue Lodges at home a
knowledge of the history of your lodge. what it has been doing . where
it has been successful. where things have not gone so well, will help you
in making your plans for the future. The same is true in your own personal life. You will be a better Mason because you look at the things of
yesterday.
My father and I had a debate on the subject, "Resolved that a young
fool is a bigger fool than an old fool." I take the affirmative and maintain
that the young fool is the bigger fool. He takes the negative and maintains that the old fool is the bigger fool. We play our own part and let
the audience decide. Dad always win! I admit it. I maintain that a young
fool is a bigger fool than an old fool because a young fool doesn't have
enough sense to learn from the old fool. If he had learned from the old
fool, he wouldn't have been a fool. Dad maintains the old fool is a bigger
fool than the young fool because the old fool doesn't even have enough
sense to learn from his own past experience. If he had learned his lesson.
he wouldn't still be a fool. It is good to learn from those who have gone
on ahead.

10

For our devotions this morning I want to read a portion of God's
Word. I will read from the third chapter of the book of Kings I: "And
King Solomon went to Gideon to sacrifice .there. In Gideon ~he Lor?
appeared to Solomon by night and God said, Ask what I sh~ll give thee .
And Solomon said, " Thou hast shown unto thy servant David. my father.
great loving kindness accordi ng as he walked before thee in truth and in
righteousness and in uprightness of heart, and now 0 Lord my God thou
hath made thy servant king and I am but a little child. I know not how
to go out or come in . And thy servant is king in the midst of a great
people that cannot be numbered nor counted because of multitudes. Give
thy ser vant, therefore, an understanding heart to judge thy people
that I may discern between good and evil.' And the words pleased the
Lord and God said, " Because thou hast asked this thing and not asked
for thyself long life. neither hast thou as ked riches for thyself. behold I
have done according to thy word. Lo I have given thee a wise and
understanding heart. so that there hath been none like thee before thee ,
neither after thee shall any rise like unto thee. And I have given thee
riches and honor, and if thou wilt walk in my ways, to keep my s tatutes
and my commandments as thy father David did walk. then I will lengthen
thy days."
I am always happy to be around Masons, for as Masons we are
young in heart and look ahead in life. No builder is living in the p~s~. A
builder always is planning for tomorrow, or he would not be bu1ldmg.
The spirit of the Masonic Lodge is looking ahead to the future. Our
interest in public schools indicates our forward look. Youth lives in the
future. Old age lives in the past. Those of us who have reached middle
a ge have stopped growing at both ends and are growing in the middle. I
knew I had reached middle age when my wife patted me on the tummy
and said, " Suck it in!" just after I had done it.
Solomon was a young man. He was looking ahead. God gave him
an opportunity to have anything he wanted. and he looked ahead to see
what he would want.

12

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Young King Solomon looked at his father's experiences and learned
that when his father had obeyed God and h<1d walked righteously before
God the armies were victorious and the people were prosperous. and
there was happiness in the land. But he also learned, because his father
was not a perfect man. that when his father disobeyed God the armies
were defeated and there was unhappiness a mong the people. It is a good
thing for us to learn the rules and then learn to play the game according
to the rules. When we obey and play according to God's divine rules the
whole universe is on our side. When we are breaking the laws all of
nature is against us.
Learn the lessons from yesterday before it is too late. A young man
went out to work on a farm. He had never been on a farm before. The
farmer put him to work hoeing weeds. Across the fence was the farmer's
mule grazing. and the mule had eaten up all the grass on his side of the
fence so the city kid brought the mule through the gate and out into the
open pasture where there were a lot of weeds . but there was nothing to
tie the mule's rope to there. So he tied the mule's rope around his own
waist, and went on hoeing while the mule went on grazing. Soon a car
came down the road and tooted its horn. scared the mule. and the mule
went clipping across the pasture dragging the city kid behind him on the
·end of the rope. When they got the mule stopped and picked the kid
up to see if he was injured. the farmer said, " Will you tell me why under
the sun you tied that rope around your waist?" The kid said. "You know.
that mule hadn't taken more than three jumps before I had seen my mistake!"
Why wait until the rope is around your neck before you learn the
lesson? Then this young king, after he had learned the lesson from his
father's experience. looked at the problems he faced. Read the record,
and you'll find that he said to God, "Thou hast made thy servant king
over a people that are beyond numbering because of multitude." He
realized the problem he faced. He knew the strength of the armies of the
surrounding enemy nations. He knew what he was going to have to do,
as king. It is a good thing for you to know what you are going to have
to do before you ask what you want for the future. Look at your own
lodge. Look at your own life. What are your problems? What a re your
responsibilities? What is going to have to be accomplished?
Third, young King Solomon looked in. He had learned the lessons
from the past. He knew the problems he faced. and now he said. "And
what has God already given me with which to solve these problems? If
you are going to ask for something you had better see what you have
already got." And so he took a look at himself and was humble. The
Scriptures tell us that he said. "J am but as a little child." It is good for
us to look at ourselves. and generally it helps us to stay humble. If you
know yourself, you are in a better position to make a request of God for
what you want in the future.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

13

One of the toughest jobs a preacher has is to get people who are in
difficulty and trouble to look at themselves. Ninety per cent of the people
who are in trouble think the trouble lies outside of themselves, in surrounding circumstances over which they seem to have no control. when
in truth the trouble lies in their own hearts and souls. If they know what
is wrong on the inside that is one area that they do have control over,
and they can decide what their attitude is going to be. Take a look at
yourself.
A negro went into a drugstore, asked the clerk if he could use the
phone, and getting permission. he called his number and the clerk heard
his end of the conversation. "Is this Mrs. Brown? I saw in the paper a
couple of weeks ago you were advertising you wanted a chauffeur. Oh.
you got one? Well. is the chauffeur that you got satisfactory? There's
nothing wrong with him? All right." And he hung up. The clerk said, "I
thought you had a job." He said, "I sure have. That's my boss. I was just
checking up on myself!"
It is a good thing for us to check up on ourselves and see what we
are and what we are becoming. The same thing is true of your local
lodge. The same thing is true of the Grand Lodge. Take a look at what
we are as of now. and what direction we ought to go in to do the job that
is ours to do.
Young King Solomon was now ready to make his request. Turning to
God. who offered to give him anything he wanted, he said, "Let me have
wisdom." Most of us stop there and think that is all Solomon asked for
-just wisdom. But Solomon defined the kind of wisdom that he wants.
He said, " Let me have a mind keen to discern good from evil. Let me
have an understanding heart to love the right and hate the wrong." It is
one thing to know what is right. and another thing to like it. It is one
thing to know what is wrong. and another thing to hate it. Solomon was
wise enough to ask for both a keen mind and a pure heart.
Here Solomon gets the answer to the problems of happiness in life.
If you want to be happy here is the answer. He also gets the answer as
to how to succeed in life. If you want to be successful here is the secret.
He also tells us how to have the right kind of a lodge. and to be the right
kind of men. Look at it carefully with me.
First. he wants a mind to know right from wrong. You may say that
is just an old fashioned conscience. Yes. but we do not have old
fashioned consciences nowadays. We have modern consciences. The
old fashioned conscience told us when we were doing wrong. A modem
conscience tells us when our neighbors are doing wrong! How can you
expect to be happy if you don't know what makes you happy? How can
you expect to be successful if you don't know what will make you successful? How can you expect to have the right kind of lodge if you do not
have the high ideals and the high standards that make a good lodge
possible? How can you drive down the highway safely if you don't know
a red light from a green light?

But if you learn to like what is good for you, and then do it. you'll be
happy. If you lea rn to like what will bring success, you can do it and life
is successful. If you learn to like what is the finest and the best and the
highest in Masonry then your Masonic activities are helpful, and you
enjoy them at the same time.
This is the secret of success and the secret of happiness. Learn to
know what is good for you , a nd learn to like it. You are going to have in
your life what you want. You don' t want scarlet fever, s mallpox, so you
quarantine them. You do like flowers , radios, and friends, and you bring
them around you. You a re going to have what you give your life to. If
you will give yourself in full devotion to an objective, that is going to be
the outcome of your life.
A bee comes in over Los Angeles. passes up all the river bottom.
marketing . business section, and finds a flower out in a garden out in a
residential district, gets a drop of honey from the flower, and a beeline
back to the hive. A buzzard comes in over Los Angeles and passes up all
the parks. the gardens, the beauty spots. sails down over the river bottom. spots the ca rcass of a dead rat, goes down and gets it. and off it goes.
They both came into town the same day. They both came and got what
they had a taste for. And you'll get in this old world whatever you have
a taste for.
If I could take you men to Chicago, or N ew York. where you are not
known . and turn you loose, and tell you to do as you please. no one would
ever know the difference- I could tell in five minutes what kind of men
you are by what you go a fter. There'd be some bees among you, but
there'd be plenty o f buzzards, too!
Wha t you a re ri ght now depends upon the decisions that you have
made in the past ten yea rs. There is a man out there ten years from now
who doesn't have any say about wha t he is going to be. You make the
decisions now, and he'll be what you want him to be. A young man went
to New York City to fin d employ ment. H e failed to find it for a week or
two and was a bit discouraged. Finally a contractor gave him a job as a
contractor's apprentice. H e learned the carpentry trade. but was not
content with that only. He went to night school. studied architecture,

CEREMON IES

This year has been filled with ceremonie s. Fourteen lodges were
constitute d. Eight lodges were instituted, ten temples were dedicated.
ten cornerston es were laid for new temples, two cornerston es were laid
for new public buildings. eight new public school buildings were dedicated and seven cornerston es were laid for new public school buildings .
A det<Jiled list is attached to this message as an exhibit. I am particular ly
pleased by the number of public school ceremonie s. which demonstra tes
a recognitio n of our support of these great American institution s. You
will also recognize from the foregoing that Freemaso nry is growing and
building, demonstra ting its virility and activity.
INSPECTORS AND GRAND LODGE OFFICERS

I cannot go further without expressing my thanks and appreciati on

The Deputy Grand Master, Senior Grand Warden and Grand Marshal

to see these faithful brethren in there pitching.
Another special kind of appreciati on goes to our Grand Secretary

and always ready to help. Our Assistant Grand Secretary, Wors hipful
Henry D. Oliphant. is a most able assistant and the office staff a credit
to this Grand Lodge.
A special word must be said about one Grand Lodge Officer, and I

For thirteen years he has performed outstandin gly not only at the

everything would be taken care of.

FIDDLETOWN CEM ETERY

In the report of the Special Committee on Cemeteries reported on
Page 28 l of the 1957 Proceedings it was recommended that title to the
old cemetery of St. Mark's Lodge No. 85 at Fiddletown, s hould be
cleared and trans ferred to Grand Lodge. The Judge Advocate has been
investigating this title. but has not been able to submit a final report.
Accordingly. this matter should be referred to the incoming Grand
Master for completion.

THE DEDICATION OF OUR NEW TEM PLE

It is our great privilege to dedicate this beautiful new California
Masonic Memorial Temple erected in memory of our brethren who
lost their lives for their country and the cause of freedom. This is our
new home. a thing of beauty. a living testimonial to the strength and
vitality of our great Fraternity.
We extend to our many distinguished visitors from va rious parts of
the world our most sincere and fra ternal greetings. We thank them for
taking time from their busy lives to be with us and hope they will
thoroughly enjoy their stay with us.
I am personally deeply indebted to Past Grand M aster L. Harold
(Pete) Anderson for the tremendous amount of time and thought which
he has put into the arrangements for this dedication and various other
matters pertaining to this Communication. Pete and his committee on
Dedication Arrangements, the Distinguished Guests Committee, the
Grand Lodge Week Activities Committee. and the Correspondence
Committee have worked together and provided hospitality and a program you will all enjoy. Elsie Wilson. wife of our Grand Secretary,
deserves the credit for a program of hospitality to the wives of our
distinguished visitors. I wish I had time to name them all. You brethren
should look at the membership of these committees and express your
personal thanks as you have the opportunity.

Again Judge Newcomb Candee and his committee have rendered to
you a great service. a labor of love which has produced an outstanding
Grand Lodge publication. One hundred ninety lodges subscribed for
all their members this past year. Those lodges and brethren who do not
read this interesting and enlightening magazine are missing something.
My hat is off to Judge Candee and his Correspondence Committee.
Tireless workers!
OuR MASONIC HoMES

Our Masonic Homes are our best known charity. There we have the
privilege and pleasure of smoothing out the path of life for about 350
of our elderly brethren, their wives and widows, and of building a
foundation upon which about 70 boys and girls can erect fu ture lives
as good. industrious American citizens. The contributions to our Endowment Fund have greatly increased this year. and I congratulate you
brethren on this achievement. Let's keep on building for the future.
The demands on our hospital facilities at Decato have outgrown the
available space. Accordingly. the trustees have started to prepare plans
for a new building, modern and up-to-date, where those requiring hospital care can be proper ly taken care of. This is a great s tep forward.
CHARLES ALBERT ADAMS

Under our law P ast Grand Master Charles Albert Adams must
ret ire as a Trustee of our Masonic Homes. He has served this Grand
Lodge long and faithfully. He was elected Grand Master in 19 19. He
inaugurated Public Sc hools Week , now grown from a program of this
Grand Lodge to a national observance to support one of A merica's
greatest traditions. He has served as a trustee of our Masonic Homes .
our greatest charity. for 40 years. Y ou'll hear more about Charlie Adams
this week. For now, I'll just say" 1\11 honor to his name!"

DECISIONS

RECOMMENDATIONS

1. I recommend that the incoming Grand Master be authorized to
appoint Past Gra nd Master Charles Albert Adams, a trustee emeritus
of the Board of Trustees of Masonic Homes of California and that the
said Board of Trustees be authorized and requested to create this office
induding the privilege of attending all meetings of the Board of Trustees.
2. I recommend that the Grand Lecturer or an Assistant Grand
Lecturer be sent to the Hawaiian Islands every two years commencing
in 1960 to hold schools of instruction for the Inspectors and officers of
the lodges in these islands.
3. I recommend that legislation be adopted to supplement Section
346. C.M.C. and provide for the forfeiture of all contributions of an
applicant who fails to come forward to be initiated within three months
after his election to receive the degrees if his fees are forfeited under
said Section 346. C.M.C.
4. I recommend that Section 332.2. C.M.C., requiring social clubs
and other groups to register with the Grand Secretary be either (a)
repealed, or, ( b) amended to permit the Grand Master. on a showing
of reasonable cause, to relieve an organization and its members from the
penalty provided in this section and to allow the registration to be made
within a specified period. This section is a trap for the innocent and a
time-consumer in the Grand Secretary's office and 1 do not feel it is
necessary.
5. I recommend that the Special Committee on Local Temple Association Finances be continued to work with and advise the trustees and
directors of our many temples to bring about more financial stability and
preparation for the future.
DECISIONS

It has been necessary to render a large number of decisions this year.
one of the most important of which was the recognition of the Grand
Lodge of Japan. I will only report the decisions which are on matters
not already covered by the California Masonic Code. Full copies of the
decisions have been furnished to the Grand Secretary. the Judge Advocate. and the Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes Committees. Sometimes I thought the brethren lay awake nights thinking up
questions for me to answer wheR they could have looked in the Code.
I tried to work out practical and workable answers.
I have digested my decisions in short question and answer form for
reporting to you as follows:

25

1. Question: Are contributions by a candidate forfeited under Sec.
546, C.M.C .. or must they be refunded under Sec. 286 and 287,
C.M.C. and particularly under 286a, 346c, and 546c.

Answer: The decision reported as 546c was repealed by the amendment in 1956 to Sec. 241, Ross Digest. now 546 C.M.C. C ontributions by the candidate are forfeited with the fees under Sec. 546,
C.M.C. Contributions are refunded under Sec. 286 and 287
C.M.C.
2. Question: Should we recognize the M.W. Grand Lodge F. & A.M.
of Japan?

Answer: We should recognize the M.W. Grand Lodge F. & A.M.
of Japan.
3. Question: I was asked to approve a Masonic Golf Tournament proposed to be held annually.

Answer: I replied that it was the policy of Grand Lodge not to give
formal approval to such outside activities, but that I saw no objection to the tournament if it was handled in a proper manner and in
compliance with our laws.
4. Question: Must all members of a committee appointed to investigate
an objection made to the advancement of a candidate file one report
as a committee report. or, may each individual member of the committee report his findin gs to the lodge at the same or different stated
meetings?

Answer: The individual members of the committee may make separate reports at the same or different stated meetings.
5. Question: May a lodge purchase from its general funds and present
a United States flag and its staff to a public school within the
jurisdiction of the lodge?

Answer: Support of our public schools is a program required by
Grand Lodge, and under Sec. 410, C.M.C .. such a purchase and
presentation could be made, but the expenditure should be limited
to an appropriate amount.
6. Question : May Job's Daughters, Rainbow Girls, and DeMolay sell
candy, cookies or Christmas trees to the public?
Answer: Yes. These youth groups do not have salaries or other
income with which to pay dues and the expenses of their organizations, and accordingly a different rule should apply to them so far
as these activities are concerned. However, the price should always
be fair and no pressure should be used to make sales.

26

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

7. Question: May table prizes be given at a card party?
Answer: Yes. but only if the prize is of nominal value such as
candy, and only if the prizes are donated by a member of the
organization or the organization itself. Door prizes may not be
given if any charge is made for participation in the card party.
8. Question: May door prizes be given at dinners and similar affairs?

Answer: Yes, but only if the prize is of nominal value such as
candy, and only if the prizes are donated by a member of the
organization. and only if no charge is made for admission to the
affair except the usual charge of the restaurant or other organization
serving the dinner or similar affair.
9. Question: Must members of an investigating committee on an application for membership in a lodge be members of the lodge to which
the application was made?

Answer: Yes. If the committee needs information from other localities. it may contact the necessary people in the other localities for
the information.
10. Question: What is the status of Wake Island?

Answer: Wake Island is open territory and a sufficient group of
Masons on that island may petition for a dispensation to form a
new lodge there.
11. Question: Does Question 13 of the form of application for the
degrees prevent a Mason from joining a club, the purpose of which
is to form a new lodge, before he has complied with the requirements of Question 137

Answer: Yes.
12. Question: May Masonic Temple Associations rent space in a
Masonic Temple to the Royal Order of Caritas or the Amaranth
Foundation?
Answer: No. The edict of P.G.M. L. Harold Anderson dated May
28, 1957, was approved by Grand Lodge and is still in full force
and effect. Amaranth Foundation should not be confused with the
Order of the Amaranth. They are entirely different organizations.
13. Question: May Masons whose wives belong to the Royal Order of
Caritas attend social functions, including refreshments after meettings, of this organization?
Answer: No. Any attendance by Masons at any function of the
Royal Order of Caritas lends some color of approval of this group.
14. Question: May organizations requiring Masonic affiliation as a
condition for membership hold dinners, teas, card parties, bazaars,

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

27

and similar activities, and invite their friends, and if so, under what
conditions?

Answer: Yes. These affairs may be held in Masonic Temples or
elsewhere, but should always be handled well within the bounds of
propriety. Members of the organization may invite their friends,
but no invitation to attend may be extended to the public as such.
There may be a news story in the local press to the effect that
the organization is having a dinner or whatever the event may be,
but this story may not refer to any charge for the affair and may
not indicate that the public is invited to attend.
Merchants or other members of the public may not be solicited
to buy tickets. participate, or make donations of any kind.
15. Question: May organizations requiring Masonic affiliation as a
condition for membership hold rummage sales, and if so, under
what conditions?
Answer: Yes, but these sales may not be held in a Masonic Temple.
The place of the sale may not display the name of the organization
conducting the sale. Any news story or advertisement may not
contain the name of the organization holding the sale. Merchants or
other members of the public may not be solicited for merchandise
or other donations to the sale.
16. Question: What lodge action, if any, is required to have a candidate
coached or examined in another lodge in this jurisdiction?

Answer: If the candidate is to be examined in another lodge, then
the lodge should by vote request the other lodge to coach and
examine th'e candidate. If the candidate is to be examined in his
own lodge, the Master may authorize or request that the candidate
be coached by a qualified member of another lodge.
17. Question: May a lodge establish a revolving fund for use of the
stewards in providing refreshments, the fund to be replenished
monthly based upon expenditures approved by the lodge?
Answer: Yes, but the stewards would be responsible for the payment of any expenditures not approved by the lodge, must render
a monthly accounting to the lodge for its approval and the fund
should never be larger than the estimated monthly requirements.
18. Question: May a lodge establish a revolving fund for the use of the
Secretary for incidental. small purchases or emergency purchases?
Answer: No. The Master should take the responsibility for necessary purchases.
19. Question: May an application for the degrees be received from an
applicant who has been out of California more than a year immediately preceding the application but whose permanent residence
has been in California during the preceding year?

28

Answer: Yes. It is up to the lodge to determine whether or not they
can make a satisfactory investigation. I recommend that the last
sentence of Sec. 517s be deleted.
20. Question: May an application be received from an applicant previously convicted of a felony but whose conviction was subsequently
reversed or set aside?

Answer: Yes. If the conviction was reversed or set aside, he was
not convicted.
21. Question: Does Section 3 ( c) of Section 403, C.M.C. permit investment of lodge funds in savings accounts and investment certificates
issued by building and loan associations and savings and loan associations organized under the statutes of Hawaii?

Answer: Yes, there is nothing in our law prohibiting members from
donating entertainment to the organization.
25. Question: ls it proper to announce to the group the name and business of the member who sponsored the entertainment?

Answer: Yes. It is common practice to do this when introducing a
speaker and the same practice would apply to the member furnishing entertainment.
26. Question: May a California lodge give a waiver of jurisdiction to
permit a resident within the jurisdiction of the lodge to apply to a
lodge in. another state?

Answer: Yes, at the request of the applicant and in favor of a
particular lodge in the other state.

Answer: Yes, if insured and otherwise in compliance with th.i.5
section.

27. Question: Is it proper for a lodge or temple association to allow a
tenant, for example, a lecturer, to post placards and other advertising material on the outside of the building?

22. Question: Does the prohibition of Question 13 of the Application

Answer: No. This is inconsistent with the dignity which should
surround any Masonic Temple.

for Degrees contained in Section 527, C.M.C., apply to Square
Clubs, High Twelve Clubs, social clubs, and similar social organizations which do not confer degrees and do not have formal
initiation ceremonies?

Answer: No. The resolution on this subject adopted in 1955 (Proceedings, pages 95 and 347) controls this question.
23. Question: I was asked to construe Sections 332.1 and 332.2.

Answer: Sec. 332.1 applies to organizations requiring Masonic
affiliation as a condition for membership and which have a ritual
or confer degrees. It prevents such organizations not established
and organized in California or Hawaii from establishing groups or
organizing in California or Hawaii. However, it does not require
members of these prohibited organizations who live in California or
Hawaii to resign their memberships elsewhere. It does not prohibit
the organization of new groups by established organizations, for
example. new Scottish Rite, York Rite. Shrine, Eastern Star, and
other established groups or new Shrine Clubs, Eastern Star clubs,
etc.. organized or chartered by or under the control of existing
organizations.
Sec. 332.2 applies to social clubs and clubs formed for the purpose of instituting a new lodge. It does not apply to organizations
having a ritual or conferring degrees or to clubs organized or
chartered by such an organization, for example, Shrine Clubs.
24. Question: Is it proper for a Shrine Club or other organization to
have entertainment at their meetings sponsored by a member and
without cost to the organization?

28. Question: Which lodge should pay the expenses of a trial the result
of which is reversed and sent back for retrial due to the failure of
the trial lodge to follow the procedural requirements of our law?

Answer.: The lodge in which the accused held membership should
not be penalized by the failure of the lodge to which the trial was
assigned to follow the proper trial procedure and the lodge which
conducted the trial should bear the cost of the first trial which was
declared to b"e a nullity.
29. Question: ls a tiler present at a lodge meeting even though he is not
in the lodge room but is in the tiler's room?

Answer: Yes.
30. Question: How should lodge minutes show which officers are present and who is acting in the meeting?

Answer: The minutes should recite which of the elected and appointed officers are present and if the Master appoints other than
such officers to fill stations or places for the meeting or for the
conferring of a degree, the minutes should recite who was so
appointed and for what business or degree.
31. Question: May lodge r~cords be microfilmed?

Answer: Yes. but only if Masons only may see or read those records
during the processing.
32. Question: Is an airplane steward who. as a small part of his duties,
assists the stewardesses in mixing and serving drinks on the plane
eligible for membership?

30

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Answer: Yes. He is not a bartender under Sec. 5 l 3a and b since
his duties include many other activities and this activity is a very
minor part.
33. Question: May an organization requiring Masonic affiliation as a
condition for membership sell charity stamps to its members?
Answer: Yes. The public is not involved and the funds go to a
recognized charity.
34. Question: May members of a group formed to ask for a dispensation for a new lodge but whose names do not appear on the dispensation be elected to membership in the new lodge after its Institution
without filing applications for affiliation. being invesitgated and
voted upon under Sec. 431 and 557, C.M.C.?
Answer: No. They must file applications for affiliation the same as
any other Mason.
35. Question: Is an applicant eligible who, at the age of 19, pleaded
guilty to a felony, was fined and placed on probation, which was
complied with, and who has since lived properly and comes well
recommended?
Answer: Yes. under Sec. 511 h, C.M.C., a youthful error which did
not show depravity, viciousness, or lack of fundamental morals
does not disqualify the applicant when his subsequent conduct has
shown him to be a good citizen of good character.
36. Question: May the constituent lodges contribute from their general
funds toward the expense of disseminating information with regard
to Proposition 16 on the November 4, 1958 California ballot?
Answer: Yes. Under Section 331, C.M.C.. state-wide public
schools welfare is a proper subject for discussion in lodges, and
und er Section 331 a, Proposition 16 was declared by Grand Lodge
to be a matter of state-wide public school welfare within the meaning of this Section. Under Section 410, C.M.C .. the expenditure of
funds for any program required by the Grand Lodge or the Grand
Master shall be deemed to be a part of the necessary expenses of
the lodge. The support of our public schools and their protection
has long been a program of this Grand Lodge. and the preparation
and dissemination of material and in formation to enable the brethren to intelligently discuss Proposition 16 and to enable them and
others to understand the facts and issues involved is a proper
expense of the lodges and they may contribute from their general
funds to a fund to be used for these purposes.
37. Question: I was asked to rule on whether or not the Order of the
Sword of Bunker Hill was in existence in our jurisdiction prior to

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

31

September 27, 1957, under Section 332.1, C.M.C.
Answer: I requested the Grand Secretary to secure further informatio~ w~th regard to the suggestion that a group representing this
orgamzat10n had been actively in existence at Hayward and to also
point out to this organization that their ritual contained matters
which should not be printed and disseminated in the California
jurisdiction and that the accuracy of some of the historical matter~
therein should be checked. No further information has been submitted, and accordingly on the basis that no proof had been furnished of existence prior to September 27, 1957 in the California
jurisdiction, I ruled that this organization did not comply with the
requirements of Section 332. l, C.M.C.
38. Question: I was asked to rule as to whether or not Section 332.1.
C.M.C.. applied to Tabernacles of the Holy Royal Arch Knight
Templar Priests.
Answer: I was advised that membership is by invitation only with
the prerequisites of certification of good standing in a recognized
regular commandery with Past Commander status. Since I had
previously ruled that Section 332.1, C.M.C., applied only to new
organizations requiring Masonic affiliation as a condition to membership and which have a ritual or confer degrees and did not apply
to organizations organized by and under the control of existing
organizations authorized to exist in the California ju.r isdiction under
this Section. it is my decision that this organization could organize
Tabernacles in the jurisdiction of California.

LODGE DUES

While I'm talking about finances , I would also suggest that you officers of lodges take a good look at your lodge's budget and financial report. A lot of you will find that you are dependent on a continuing group
of candidates to make ends meet. In other words, you will be in trouble
if you do not get a s teady stream of applicants for the degrees.
If you are to be in a sound financial condition, you should be able to
live 011 your dues and put aside a big share of the candidates' fees as a
reserve for the future. I know it isn't popular to raise dues. but it's good
sense if you can't Jive on your present dues. It's worth studying and
thinking about. Plan for your future, not just for today.
TAX EXEMPTION

There has been so much misleading and incorrect propaganda put
out by those w ho favor tax exemption for private and parochial schools
that it has been necessary to secure and distribute material to give you
the facts. Proposition 16 on your November ballot will repeal the tax
exemption now enjoyed by these private and parochial schools. As citizens you are enjoined to study this issue and learn all you can about it.
Tax exemption is a public subsidy requiring taxpayers to pay more
public taxes for the benefit of private progra ms. This is not the American Way. Why should you personally and your Temples pay more
taxes to help private schools indoctrinate children in a particular faith?
In America we select and support the church and faith of our choice and
we should not force others to pay more taxes to support private school
programs of our church or faith.
Every child in America can a ttend the public schools supported by
everyone. These public schools have made and kept these United Stat~s
a self-governing land of freedom . These public schools have taugoht our
children to live and work with children of all religious faiths and from
all walks of life regardless of race or wealth. Public schools weld our
people into a united group. private and parochial schools divide our
people by religious faiths or wealth. Furthermore. published surveys
show that public school students get a better education than students of

CONCLUSION

The Engliih language is entirely inadequate to express to you, my
brethren, the pleasure and the pure happiness I have experienced this
past year. Only the privilege of meeting and working with the members
of this great fraternity can bring these great rewards of friend!!hip with
and fraternal love and affection to others. Wonderful and lasting memories of kindness. hospitality and good fellowship come flooding over
me as I close this report of my year as your Grand Master. I wish I
could find the words to express to you my gratitude for the privilege and
honor you have given to me. I can only hope that you can read between
the lines and see into my heart, for there you will find indelible pictures
of all of you.
May I close with this ancient and hallowed Masonic benediction :

" M ay no strife disturb thy days, nor sorrow disturb
thy nights, and may the pillow of peace kiss thy cheek.
and the pleasures of imagination attend thy dreams; and
when length of years hath made thee tired of earthly joys.
and the curtains of death gently close around the scene of
thy existence, may the angels of God attend thy bed and
take care that the expiring lamp of life shall not receive
even one rude blast to hasten its extinction; and finally
may the blessing of God wash thee free from all impurities
and prepare thee to enter into the land of everlasting
happiness.··

PROCLAMATION OF TH E GRAND MASTER
CALIFORNIA FREEMASON
We hope that every member of the Lodges in this jurisdiction will
become a subscriber to the California Freemason . It is owned and published by your Grand Lodge to bring you Masonic information and
inspiration.
It is especially important that the brother who for various reasons is
not able to keep in close touch with his Lodge receive this magazine. It
will pay for itself in s timulating greater interest and participation in
Lodge activities.
At the last Communication, the representatives of the Lodges voted
to authorize the Lodges to pay for a subscription for each of their
members. Heretofore this payment had to be made from the refreshment
fund. Grand Lodge now considers the cost of the California Freemason
a justified and wise expenditure of Lodge funds .
I ask that each Lodge consider this proposition at its December
stated meeting. To do so in the proper manner, the following resolution
is suggested :
RESOLVED that the California Freemason be sent to each member of this Lodge, the cost to be pa id in January of each year on receipt
of a bill from the Grand Secretary at the rate of not to exceed 60c per
member as shown in the last annual return.
If the resolution is adopted . the secretary of the Lodge will certify
the same to the Grand Secretary within 15 days and furnish h im with
a list of the names and addresses of the members of the Lodge.
If the resolution fails adoption , the secretary will notify the Grand
Secretary within the same period so that we may know how each Lodge
feels on the subject.
The regular subscription price, if not paid through the Lodge, will
remain at $I per year.
I DIRECT THAT THIS COMMUNICATION BE READ AT
THE DECEMBER STATED MEETING.
October 29. 1957
Attest :
LLOYD E . w ILSON
Grand Secretary

LEO E . ANDERSON
Grand Master

December 12, 1957

To the Lodges and Members of this Jurisdiction:
You will recall that last year Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderson
issued an edict prohibiting Masons subject to the jurisdiction of the
Grand Lodge of California from being, becoming. or remainin~ a
member of the Royal Order of Caritas or of the Amaranth Foundation,
Inc .. or their successors.
It has come to my attention that there exists considerable confusion
as to whether or not this edict refers to the Order of the Amaranth.
The Order of the Amaranth is an entirely different organization
from the Amaranth Foundation or the Royal Order of Caritas. and the
edict does not apply to the Order of the Amaranth.
This communication shall be read in Lodge at the stated meeting
next following its receipt, and I trust it will end the confusion which
now exists.
Fraternally yours.
LEO

Attest :
LLOYD E. WILSON

PROCLAMATION
THIRTY-NINTH ANNUAL PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

The week of April 21 throug h April 26. 1958. has been designated
as the thirty-ninth annual Public Schools Week in California.
The theme for this year's celebration is " Public Schools. the Foundation of American Freedom ."
Our interest in our public schools is of long standing and constitutes
one of our most important activities. We could not govern ourselves and
protect our American freedoms if the people of these United States did
not receive the fu ndamental education given through our public schools.
Good public schools supported by an informed public assure good citizenship.
This will be an important year in the history of the Public Schools of
California. This year the voters of California will determine whether or
not all citizens regardless of religious faith will be fo rced to pay taxes to.
support parochial schools teaching a faith they may or may not agree
with.
The public schools are the foundation of America's greatness and its
high standard of living. Support them. protect them, and maintain your
interest in them throughout the year, but particularly during Public
Schools Week.
''Next in importance to freedom and justice is popular
education, without which neither freedom nor justice can be
permanently maintained." President Ja mes A. Garfield. July 12. 1880
This Proclamation shall be read a t the stated meetings in the months
of March and April. 1958.
Dated : January 31, 1958.
Attest :
LLOYD E. WILSON

Grand Secretary

LEO E. ANDERSON

Grand Master

MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT MONT H

The month of May is again designated as Masonic Homes Endowment Month.
Those brethren who have had the privilege of visiting either our
Home at Decoto for our elderly brethren. their wives and widows, or

These homes are made possible by the contributions made by the
bre thren of this Jurisdiction and many sojourning brethren who like to
join in this pleasant work. Those who give may be proud of the record of
the Masons of California in caring for these guests of ours.

p ROCLA MA TION
CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE MoNTH
On the 17th day of September, 1787, in Independence Hall in the
City of Philadelphia, a group of patriotic Americans, great men in history, signed their names to the Constitution of the United States of
America. Twenty-three of the thirty-nine who signed this charter of
freedom were known or believed to be Masons.
This great charter of freedom has given to us more happiness, more of
the good things of life, more of the inalienable rights of men than any
other country in history. Because of this charter of freedom we are the
most fortunate people in all the world.
It is therefore appropriate that during the month of September we
turn our thoughts to our blessings and celebrate as a patriotic festival
the anniversay of the adoption of our Constitution.
I therefore designate the month of September 1958 as Constitution
Observance Month. I direct that in observance thereof every Lodge of
this Jurisdiction, preferably in conjunction with other Lodges. Masonic
Districts, service clubs, and public groups, shall sponsor or hold a special
meeting open to the public during this month at which a program suitable
to the occasion shall be given and that every effort be made to secure the
attendance of the families, friends, and neighbors of the brethren as well
as the public generally.
Reverence for our Constitution and eternal vigilence are the basis of
American liberty.
This Proclamation shall be read at each stated meeting during the
months of July and August. l 958.

Grand Master: In order to give you a better understa nding of our
participa tion in this program , permit me to go back into history.
The Masons of Californ ia have on many occasion s demonst rated
their interest in the public schools of this state and nation. Among the
demonst rations of that interest, we may point to the annual observan ce
of Public Schools Week, which was conceive d and inaugura ted by one
of our Grand Masters shortly after World War I. During that week.
all Masonic Lodges througho ut the state refrain from all other activities .
and devote their efforts to focusing public attention upon our public
schools. Governo rs. mayors and other officials have proclaim ed the
?bserva~ce. a~d join in urging visitation s to our public schools and
public
mterest m their work and needs. The observan ce, as was intended . has
become a commun ity affair. but the impetus and certain arrangem ents
come from our lodges.
This associati on of public schools and the Masonic Fraterni ty did
not originate with Public Schools Week, but has its roots in a far earlier
period of America n history.
George Washing ton, Benjamin Franklin , Paul Revere, and scores of
others who worked and fought to achieve our national independ ence.
were officers of Masonic Lodges. They, and those who came after
them, built this nation upon a cornersto ne of universa l public educatio n.
Our founding fathers realized that if the nation they launched was to
survive and become strong. it must rest upon adequate and widespre ad
educatio n.
Freemas ons and other America ns of succeedi ng generati ons have
been aware that the continue d growth of our beloved country, and the
continua nce of our freedom likewise depend upon our public educatio n
system. It has been truly said that the price of liberty is eternal vigilance .
and this statemen t would apply with equal truth to the preserva tion
of our public school system.
As further historica l backgrou nd, you may be intereste d in knowing
that from earlier centuries has also come the custom of requestin g Free~
masons to lay the foundati on stones of importan t buildings . The cornerstones of our National Capitol. the White House, countles s state
capitols. and public buildings , including public school buildings . have

been laid with the ceremonies provided for such occasions. From these
early traditions and associations has come the custom of Masonic participation in this ceremony. We consider it a privilege to assemble to dedicate this building to the purposes for which it has been erected.
(We will now have another number from the..................................... )

Grand Master: It was a custom among ancient peoples to dedicate
or consecrate the work of their hands. Temples. altars and statues were
commonly dedicated or consecrated to some divinity. In some lands, the
custom was not limited to public edifices. but was extended to private
houses. It was believed that no pious or sensible man would expect to
dwell sa fely in a building that was not under the immediate protection
of God. A distinction. however. was frequently made between consecration and dedication. Sacred things were consecrated and dedicated,
while others were dedicated only.
This building is to be used for the education of our youth, and thus
for the building and preservation of our great country. It is only by
free public education that we are prepared to govern ourselves and
maintain our freedom.
I therefore dedicate this school building to TRUTH
EQUALITY (gavel). and FREEDOM (gavel) .

(gavel),

It is dedicated to TRUTH . the daughter of Almighty God, because
Truth is knowledge and must ever be the object of true education .
Truth is, because it is; not because men say so. It does not. emanate
from the declaration of any man or group of men of those things which
they wish to believe. It emanates from the act of creation by the Great
Architect of the Universe. The ascertainment of Truth, regardless of
the effect upon preconceived beliefs. and regardless of creeds and
dogmas, must ever be the goal of all true seekers after knowledge.
Whenever the search for Truth. or its declaration, is made secondary to
religious creeds or dogmas or any other limitations, then is youth led
from the broad highway into bypaths.
This building is dedicated to EQUALITY, not merely because
Equality is one of the principal tenets of Freemasonry. but because it is
one of the foundation stones of our republic. Our founding fathers
wrote in their Declaration of Independence: " W e hold these truths to
be self-evident: that all men are created equal ... "
Universal public education is a manifestation and preserver of that
equality. In our public schools. youth of every race and creed are
brought together without distinction as to their beliefs. All. regardless
of material wealth, arc offered the same knowledge. the same opportunities. The doors of this building are open to all without discrimination, a
true reflection of our national dedication. Equality unites; inequality
divides. Through the equal opportunities offered to all, our public

53

!!chools draw our people together and build a better America.
This building is dedicated to FREEDOM. because Freedom can
be maintained only by an enlightened citizenry. Ignorance is the weapon
w hich tyrants and demagogues use to destroy liberty. Such men know
that mental darkness makes a people a blinder. more ready tool and
instrument for their purposes. The unbiased knowledge spread by the
public schools constitutes public education . the foundation and the
guarantor of our liberty. Within these walls will be taught no divided
allegiance, but an allegiance to our nation . and our national ideals . May
those who come here in search of knowledge go forth to make our
country forever "the land of the free and the home of the brave."
(Again we have the pleasure of listening to the schooL .................... )
Grand Master: Once more may we express our appreciation for the
opportunity of participating in this dedication ceremony. We congratulate you upon the completion of this beautiful school. Other nations may
have more land. others may have more people, others may have greater
natural resou rces. but we have the highest standard of living and greater
freedom, because we have a long history of public education, the largest
and best public school system in all the world and teachers and administrators dedicated to the teaching of our youth. But most important are
the students. the young men and women who will determine the future
of America. For them we build our schools. Freemasonry is soundly
behind our public schools.

MASONIC SERVICE BOARD
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. 6 A. M. of California:
Whereas: The functions, duties and operations of Masonic Boards
of Relief have been so enlarged and expanded since such Boards were
first established by this Grand Lodge so as to make the title "Board
of Relief" completely incomprehensive and inadequate as it covers only
one of the many services performed by the various Boards:
And WHEREAS: In the experience of the officers of many Boards
the term "Relief" has come to convey a meaning which is very repugnant
to sojourning Masons and their families who request or need some
Masonic service which is in no way relief or charity,
THEREFORE: For the purpose of providing a more comprehensive
and inclusive name, which does not carry the stigma of implied destitution to the minds of many receiving services which have nothing to do
with charity:
BE IT RESOLVED: That the title "Masonic Service Board" be
substituted for "Board of Relief" or "Boards of Relief," as applicable in
Sections 153, 244, 262, 263, 264, 265, 409, 601, 602, 603, 604 and their
various annotations, of the California Masonic Code and in any other
Sections of the Ordinances in which the title may appear and that all
such Sections be, and they are, hereby so amended.
EDGAR L. FEASEL, W.M.
Caledonia Lodge No. 486
TROY BRADSHAW, W.
Caledonia Lodge No. 486

MASONIC SERVICE AND EMPLOYMENT BUREAU
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, there exists in this Grand Jurisdiction eighteen Boards
of Relief and six Employment Bureaus so named in the CaLifomia
Masonic Code, and

58

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

WHEREAS. the word "RELIEF" while denoting one of the greatest tenets of Freemasonry which must be given when necessary, the
word itself has, in recent years, become closely associated with the word
"WELPARE" which is extremely distasteful to Master Masons and
their dependents who pride themselves on the fact that they are not
subjects of a so-called "WELP ARE STA TE." and
WHEREAS. the work of the several Boards of Relief in this Jurisdiction entails more service than actual relief by counseling, advising and
assisting in many ways other than direct relief, and
WHEREAS, it was regularly adopted at the Stated Meeting of
Lemon Grove Lodge No. 736 held on Monday, March 3, 1958, that
the following resolution be presented to this Grand Lodge,
THEREFORE. BE IT RESOLVED: That the name of the "MASONIC BOARD OF RELIEF AND EMPLOYMENT BUREAU,"
be and is hereby changed to "MASONIC SERVICE AND EMPLOYMENT BUREAU," and that the California Masonic Code be corrected
to show this name wherever it appears therein.
LIONEL A. THOROGOOD, Worshipful Master
Lemon Grove Lodge No. 736
WILLIAM E. RIFE, Past Master
Lemon Grove Lodge No. 736
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes, and Board of Control.

WHEREAS, page 12 of the Monitor and Officers' Manual, issued
by Grand Lodge, states in part "and since their time there is, or should
be, represented in every regular Lodge a certain point within a circle,"
and
WHEREAS, it is our sincere belief that the use of "a certain point
within a circle" does not conflict with the intent of ruling in C.M.C.,
Section 554 V, and
NOW, THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED: That the use of these
ancient anc;I accepted implements be authorized in theGrand Jurisdiction.

TO ESTABLISH "OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS FUND"

tary may designate from agencies supported in whole or in part by the
Grand Lodge.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, our Public Schools System is the foundation of our
American way of life, and
WHEREAS, Proposition No. 16, win or lose, will not be the end of
threats against our Public School System on a state-wide basis, but
will continue for years to come, and
WHEREAS, the stated meetings of our Constituent Lodges are
becoming a meeting place of committee chairmen asking for donations
for various worthwhile causes,
THEREFORE , BE IT RESOLVED: That this Grand Lodge
establish a fund to be known as "OUR PUBLIC SCHOOLS FUND";
and that a twenty-five cent per capita tax be imposed for this purpose;
and that the Grand Master appoint a committee to disperse from said
fund for the protection of our Public Schools on a state-wide basis.
WILLIAM E. RIFE, Past Master
Lemon Grove Lodge No. 736
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes.

TO AMEND SECTION 223
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
RESOLVED, that Section 223 of the Ordinances be amended by
deleting from the last sentence the words, "in an amount not to exceed
One Hundred_ Fifty Dollars ($150.00), thereby relieving the obligated
Lodge to this extent," and substituting therefor the words, "in an
amount to be determined by the Trustees, thereby relieving the obli9ated
Lodge to that extent."
The amended section would then, in the last sentence, read as
follows:
"Said Trustees shall pay the necessary burial expenses of residents
of the Masonic Homes who die while under the supervision of said
Trustees, in an amount to be determined by the Trustees, thereby
relieving the obligated Lodge to that extent."
CHARLES M. WOLLENBERG,
President Trustees, Masonic Homes
Referred to Committees on Jurisprudence, on Policy and General
Purposes.

SBVENTY -PIVE YEAR BUTTON

During the year we have had another veteran Mason achieve 75
years of membership and this time it was a resident of our Masonic
Home at Decoto.
Brother Clarence Eugene Childs, Palo Alto Lodge No. 346, was the
recipient of the seventy-five year button presente d on Novemb er 10,
1957, at Decoto by Past Grand Master L. Harold Anderso n, himself a
Past Master of Palo Alto Lodge No. 346.
FIRST MASONIC MEETING IN NEW TEMPLE

The first Masonic meeting held in the new California Masonic Memorial Temple was on Thursda y, August 21st, at 8:00 P.M., when approximately 1,200 elective and appointive Officers from the Lodges in
Alameda, Contra Costa, Marin, San Francisc o and San Mateo Counties
assembled in response to a summons from Most Worship ful Leo E. Anderson. Grand Master.
Appropr iately enough the subject of the Grand Master's discourse
was the welfare of the public schools in this state. He called upon all
present to marshal themselves and their forces for the protection of this
bulwark of America n democracy and freedom.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

AFTERNOON SESSION-Monday, September 29, 1958
At 1 :50 p.m. 1Grand Lodge was called on, the Grand Master presiding. The Grand Chaplain delivered the invocation.

DEDICATION CEREMONY
Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems, as President of the Trustees
of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, reviewed the history of
the Memorial Temple program and requested the Grand Master to
dedicate the Temple as follows:
The Grand Lodge of California, F. & A. M .. on its 109th Annual
Communication has gathered here this afternoon to dedicate the California Masonic Memorial Temple, our first headquarters wholly-owned
by the Masons of California. It is a distinct honor and privilege to present for dedication to this distinguished audience this great memorial
edifice. I feel particularly humble in making this presentation for it is
usually an act of fate and circumstances beyond human control which
make it necessary for the vice chairman of a committee to assume the
chairmanship and such an important responsibility.
Gathered here as we are with our friends and brethren from around
the globe, in this magnificent Temple erected by the Masons of California
and Hawaii as a memorial to our war dead brethren, a feeling of sincere
regret comes over those of us who know him, that our beloved Past
Grand Master Francis Valentine Keesling is not able to be present with
us today. BrothE!r Keesling was the original chairman of the building
committee. This site high upon historic Nob Hill on which this Memorial
Temple is erected, was his first choice. It was his great vision, inspiration
and enthusiasm captured by the committee that has resulted in the edifice
we present today for your inspection and dedication. Failing health
forced Brother Keesling to retire and is the cause of his absence today.
A review of the original planning and construction of the Temple
is given in the 1958 Annual Report of the Trustees to this Grand Lodge,
and will be printed in the Proceedings. Additional general information
is to be found in the dedication issue of the California Freemason.
Obviously, it would be repetitious and time consuming to review it in
its entirety. A brief historical review of the principal Masonic Temples
associated with the growth of this Grand Lodge during the first 108
years is in order.
The three-story Red House on the corner of Fifth and "J" Streets, in
Sacramento, where this Grand Lodge was formed, holds an important
place in the history in California.
Many stories have been written and repeated, and, I might add, some
with embellishment-perhaps all too many times-about the ruggedness
1

86

87

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

of pioneer days in the far West-particularly in California. Without
being critical. I have only to refer to the current issue of the California
Freemason. the lead paragraph "from the desk of the Grand Secretary,"
where he says in speaking of the Red House " ... and the second floor
inhabited by some who allegedly were not the first citizens of Sacramento." Now, I ask you, after 108 years, what does he mean and how
does he know in what business they were engaged? Obviously, my own
vivid imagination would lead me to the belief that perhaps those referred
to by the Grand Secretary might have been cattle rustlers, or it might
have been the headquarters for stage coach bandits. History books speak
freely of conditions which would justify such a conclusion.
The fact remains. my brethren, regardless of how fertile your imagination might be, it is significant that those lodges meeting in communication to form this Grand Lodge built some of that ruggedness, some of
that atmosphere, some of that philosophy into the stature of this Grand
Lodge. Certainly the real motivating factor of those men who gathered
in the Red House in the City of Sacramento in 1850 to form this Grand
Lodge was "service above self." They were truly men of good will.
They had all knelt at Masonic altars: they were men who understood
the true meaning of brotherly love, and who practiced charity. Those
men of good will laid the cornerstone of California Masonry. The Red
House isn't mentioned here because of a proprietary interest in it, for
it wasn't even partially owned by the Masons of California. But it
probably could have been for the 103 members of the three lodges forming this Grand Lodge, together with the other Masons of the area, chose
rather to build the temple of humanity in the hearts of men than to build
a physical structure in which to meet. For the record is indelibly clear
that those brethren of good will, in an effort to relieve the distressing
situation resulting from the several cholera epidemics at the time,
expended personal funds aggregating $33,000 for the relief of the needy
in a single year.
The first Masonic Temple, partially owned by Grand Lodge, was
erected in the city of San Francisco during the height of the Civil War.
It was located at Post and ·Montgomery Streets on a lot comprising
about 12,000 square feet. The cost was $250,000. The building started
in 1860 and was finished in 1870. At the time of the dedication in 1863,
prior to its final completion, the Grand Master stated, "This is the finest
and most perfect building upon the Pacific Coast, and when finished it
will be the most beautiful. if not the most expensive Masonic Temple in
America." That Temple of Romanesque-Gothic architecture with its
ornamental facades, pointed arches and slender spires served the Masons
of California for over forty years.
A further search of the record discloses that in the year 1904 the
Grand Lodge of California, experiencing unusual rapid growth, felt the
need for more extensive quarters. Our own Senior Past Grand Master

Oscar Lawler, then a member of the Finance Committee, reported that
the "demand for the acquisition of quarters sufficiently commodious to
meet the requirements is imperative."
In April, 1906, the great fire and earthquake destroyed the Masonic
Temple at Post and Montgomery Streets, and in October the lot on
which the Temple stood was sold for $750,000, and the Temple Association liquidated. That act of God, earthquake and fire, forced early
action by Grand Lodge.
In 1908 the new Association, through the Special Committee, purchased the site at 25 Van Ness Avenue. The new site comprised an area
of approximately 20,000 square feet, less than one-half the area of our
present site. The cornerstone was laid on October 11. 1911, and dedicated at the Annual Communication October 13, 1913.
It is interesting to relate that three names prominent during the
construction and dedication of the Masonic Temple at 25 Van Ness
Avenue 45 years ago are brethren who have kept an active interest in
Masonry all through the years. They are: Our Senior P.G.M. Oscar
Lawler, already referred to in this presentation and who became Grand
Master in 1908 at the age of 33 years. We have many 50-year Masons;
to have been a Grand 'Master 50 years ago is certainly the exception and
worthy of special mention on such an important occasion as this. P.G.M.
Charles Albert Adams, 91 years young next November, the originator of
our annual Public Schools Observance Week, became Grand Master in
1919. He was a director of the Masonic Temple Association, and active
in the Grand Lodge during the construction and dedication of the Temple
at 25 Van Ness Avenue; and P.G.M. Samuel E. Burke who became
Grand Master in 1921. At the time of the dedication in 1913, P.G.M.
Burke held the office of Grand Bible Bearer.
The first two are lawyers, both still practicing law. Brother Burke,
before retirement, was a dentist. All three have been distinguished civic
and Masonic records of accomplishment.
P.G.M. Lawler currently recovering from surgery is not present with
us for that reason. P.G.M. Burke has not been able to attend the past
several sessions of Grand Lodge due to failing health. But P.G.M.
Adams is present. He has built a distinguished and enviable record.
There may have been others who were active then and who may be
alive and present today, but these brethren have maintained an active
interest in the affairs of this Grand Lodge. Their influence has been
built into the structure of Freemasonry; it has also been built into the
Temple we are now about to dedicate.
My Brethren-many of us, as individuals, have felt the pride and
joy of owning our own home. The day we moved in, the feeling of
accomplishment and satisfaction is beyond description-others may
still be anticipating that experience. Masonically, for all of us that day
