ADDRESS OF THE RIGHT HONORABLE
THE EARL OF SCARBROUGH
GRAND MASTER OF THE UNITED GRAND LoDGE OF ENGLAND
Most Worshipful Grand Master, Brethren of the
Grand Lodge of California:
It is my privilege to bring to you the congratulations, warm and
sincere, of the United Grand Lodge of England on the completion of
your great endeavor by the dedication yesterday of your new California Masonic Memorial Temple.
Those congratulations I have the privilege to bring you have a
special measure of warmth in them because you have made this great
new building of yours a memorial to those of your brethren who gave
their lives in the cause of freedom. All the world knows of the valor
and the immense achievements of the armed forces of the United States.
We in England not only have that knowledge, but also some special
intimate and very cherished memories of your forces, because it was
from our shores that those allied armies-American, Canadian and
British-set sail for the liberation of Europe just over 14 years ago.
Those allied forces were under one supreme command. Many of
us have memories of our service side by side with you, and it so happens that all three of us who represent the Grand Lodge of England
here today, our Assistant Grand Master, Right Worshipful Brother
Major General Sir Allan Adair; our Grand Secretary, Very Worshipful Brother Colonel James Stubbs; and myself, had the honor of
serving under the supreme command of General Eisenhower. And so it
is with these special and intimate memories that we bring our congrat-

95

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

ulations on this great memorial achievement, and we mingle with our
congratulations our homage and the cherished memories of comra~~
.
And then, too, this memorial building of your reminds us that our
own Masonic headquarters in London, England, in Great Queen
Street, which some of you know, is also a memorial building, a memorial to those of our brethren who gave their lives in the first World
War. And so we have some recollection and understanding of the
years of thought and effort, in planning and designing and selecting,
and the raising of money which was needed before we could see
our work completed; and having that understanding, our congratulations to you are the more sincere.
Now, brethren, it has been suggested to me-I hope my information is not wrong-that you could stand it if I gave you a short
account of how Freemasonry fares in England today. Our jurisdiction comprises England and Wales, and also a number of districts
and lodges overseas, for wherever Englishmen find themselves, they
seem to sow the seeds of Masonry-in Africa, in India, Pakistan, the
West Indies, and in many other parts of the world.
To give you an idea of our jurisdiction overseas I can tell you that
within recent years I have consecrated a lodge in Pretoria, South Africa,
and have met our brethren in Singapore, New Delhi and Karachi, and
the Assistant Grand Master, who is a great traveler on Masonic matters, has been to Nigeria, Ghana, South Africa and Gibraltar, and
when he has completed his present journey he will set off for Hongkong and other places in that part of the world. We number now
some 7,000 lodges: our brethren number some 600,0~and 500,000
of those are in England and Wales and some 100,000 in our lodges
overseas.
Then I must tell of the ways by which we practice benevolence
in the shape of our care for the orphans of Masons and for old people.
We have three Masonic institutions: one for girls, one for boys and
one for old people, which for many years now have been kept up by
our brethren in the English jurisdiction. Since the war some nine million pounds have been contributed by our brethren to these institutions. We have something else in which we take some pride-our
Royal Masonic Hospital. which has a fine reputation in our medical
world. That hospital has never cost our state a cent. It has all been
built and maintained by the contributions of our brethren, and soon
after I return a large extension will be opened by Queen Elizabeth
the Queen Mother.
Those, brethren, are some facts and figures, but as you know well
in California, the story of Freemasonry cannot really be told by statistics.
We endeavor to put into practice those same Masonic ideals which
you do--brotherhood and friendship in our lodges, the practice of

benevolence, as is shown by our Masonic institutions, and so far as
we can we try to promote virtue amongst ourselves. I don't much
like talking about the Masonic virtues, lest I be led to become like the
Pharisee who thanked God that he was not as other men were. We
no doubt fail to reach the ideals, but we try to remind ourselves to put
into practice what our ritual teaches.
What does it all amount to in England? I must not exaggerate.
There are many other things in England that work for the good of
others, but I think that to have 500,000 men in England and Wales
who have been taught Masonry in our lodges is of some national
value, and I like to think that the Craft is doing something good for
our country.
But when one comes overseas to a great Masonic gathering such
as this, attended by representatives from many parts of the world, the
thought is bound to come upon us that Masonry can do good, not
only within the bounds of our own country but across the boundaries
of our jurisdictions, and I do not think there is anything quite like
Masonry for breaking the ice between people of different countriesor should I say melting the rocks. Since I have been in the United
States in the last two or three weeks I have found, in the warmth of
Masonic fellowship, many things about your country which have
been interpreted to me, and I believe we Freemasons can do quite a
lot to interpret our countries to each other. I am not suggesting, of
course, that Freemasonry should formulate a kind of foreign policy.
We leave that to our governments. We can, however, work on the
foundations which our governments must have, and help them by
interpreting ourselves to each other. Since I have had so much about
your country interpreted to me in these few days, 1 would like, in
return, to try and interpret to you two things about England. It is
true we have a country with a long history, and we have ancient
institutions, which, however, we have often been able to adapt to
new usages: and I expect many of you think of England as "Old
England" and perhaps as a country living in the past. We are proud
of our past, but you would be making a mistake if you thought that
we were just living on our past.
May I give you the other side of the picture and tell you just
one or two things which, six thousand miles away from us, may not
be easily apparent to you? In your great vast country perhaps you
have still not got all the equipment you want for it and are still making things mainly for your own use. In England we are a small island
with a large number of people in it, and we have to export if we are
going to eat. If some you have not been to England in the last six or
seven years I would like to tell you that we are eating better; and
that is because we have now doubled our exports, compared to what
they were before the war; and we export some things which may sur-

94

97

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

prise you, as indeed they surprise me. We are the greatest exporters
in the world of automobiles; and when I came through your Rocky
Mountains the other day and saw something of your great electrical
developments, I was able to remind myself that we are also the greatest
exporters of heavy electrical equipment, among other things.
I am giving you the other side of the picture. And how have these
things come about? Partly through the work of our scientists. We
have, for instance, in operation, through their skill, the first-and I
think still the largest nuclear power station in the world. In another
part of England our scientists have produced the highest temperature
ever known to man. Our scientists and our workers have helped in
things like this. Sometimes it is said that the British worker no longer
works as he used to do. In fact, he works. on the average, seven
hours a week longer than the American works. What about the
tempo of his work? Here I will call to my assistance some words recently used by the president of the Canadian Manufacturers ' Association. He said not long ago, "I have never seen such a high work tempo
in any country-Cana da and the United States included."
That is part of the other side of the picture which I am trying
to interpret to you. It is because the British worker is working as he
is doing that we are able to confront the future with confidence. Then
there are those things which lift up our morale: they may be small,
but they help. We hold the land and water speed records. From time
to time we hold the air speed record as well; then you come and take it
away from us. Then there were those two expeditions accomplished
successfully with the cooperation of our brothers in the Commonwealth-the ascent of Mount Everest, almost on the day when our
Queen was crowned, and the recent crossing of the Antarctic Continent.
We may be "Old England" but our men have still the spirit
of adventure in them, and that is part of the interpretation of England I would like to make to you. So, when you come to England to
visit us, there are other things in England which you can see besides
the changing of the guard at Buckingham Palace. We like that, and
so do you, judging by the crowds of visitors from your country I see
in the summer. But remember. there are other things in England besides the old things.
And the other interpretation which I venture to offer to you for
your consideration is what we in England think about you. In these
days many things are written and many things are said, and not all
of them wisely written or wisely said, but what really counts are
the deep thoughts, deep in the minds of people, undisturbed by the
ripples which sometimes appear on the surface. And I would interpret
to you the deep thoughts of people in England about you in this way.
We wonder at and admire your spacious land, your great concep-

tions. your vast achievements, and your generosity, unparalleled in
history, towards other peoples. And we thank the Great Architect
of the Universe that there is in this great land of yours a nation dedicated to high ideals. which preserve its might and power to keep
peace in the world and to insure that freedom shall not perish from
the earth. Those. brethren, are the true and deep thoughts in our
minds about you, and it is Freesmasonry that enables us to tell each
other our deep thoughts now and again.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, the three of us who have come
from England to represent our Grand Lodge at this communication
and to witness the dedication of your memorial temple, will never
forget these days that we are spending with you and your brethren.
We shall long remember that great Masonic day of yesterday, and in
particular the dignity and perfection of the opening of your Grand
Lodge and the dedication of the temple. We shall keep in our minds
a picture of this great building, filled to the roof with the brethren
of California. We shall not easily forget the princely hospitality
which you shower upon us and upon our wives. But most of all we
shall keep green the memory of the warmth and kindness and friendship which have lapped us round since the first moment that we set
foot in this city.
We have received much from you and your brethren in these days.
We would like to leave something behind us, something which might
be a little useful and a reminder of the Grand Lodge of England.
That was the thought of our Grand Lodge. And I have brought with
me from the Grand Lodge of England a little gift for the Grand
Lodge of California. It is only a small thing; it is, as a matter of
fact, a silver ink stand. It is of respectable age. Its date is 1783, and
it was made, as other things were made, in the days of ·G eorge III.
I believe-I may be wrong; this is my first visit to the United States! believe that George III has never enjoyed a first class reputation
in the United States. But that did not prevent the silversmiths of
London from doing some of their best work in his reign.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, we hope that this little gift of
ours may have a long sojourn in this great new building of yours. If
you think well of the suggestion that it might be used by the Grand
Masters of the Grand Lodge of California, we should be very happy.
In presenting it to you from the Grand Lodge of England there go
with it some sentiments which should ever distinguish us as men and
as Masons: there go with it the brotherly love and affection of all
the brethren in all the lodges under the Grand Lodge of England.

REPORT OF GRAND TREASURER
For the Fiscal Year Ended June 30, 1958
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
This is the fourth annual report it has been my privilege to submit
to this Grand Lodge as your Grand Treasurer.
Section 146 of the "California Masonic Code" sets forth in its simplicity the duty of the Grand Treasurer: To receive all monies belonging
to Grand Lodge from the Grand Secretary and to give a receipt therefor,
etc., only implies the volume of work done by the staff of Grand Lodge.
The record shows that about 40% of those in attendance are here for
the first time. In order for all members of Grand Lodge present to
visualize the volume of work involved, I shall again endeavor to describe
the cash flow of funds received from all sources. Receipts from all
sources sent in by the several constituent lodges are deposited by the
Grand Secretary to the credit of the Grand Treasurer in a bank account
maintained for that purpose. This is a collection or reservoir account.
To this account is also deposited such other items as funds from bequests,
proceeds of sales, etc., which are transmitted directly to the Grand
Secretary's office for the account of the Endowment Fund, the Masonic
Homes, or the Grand Lodge.
At the end of each month, after review by the auditors and with
their approval. there is withdrawn from the above reservoir account
the total of amounts belonging to the Grand Lodge, the Endowment
Fund, the Masonic Homes General Fund, or to any of the 15 special
funds of the Masonic Homes in order that such items may be deposited
to the separate accounts of these funds.
California Masonic Memorial Temple funds received from the constituent lodges, or from individuals, are deposited direct to the Temple
account. Should a check made payable to the California Masonic
Memorial Temple by a constituent lodge also include funds belonging
to some other account, a proper withdrawal is made at the end of each
month the same as though the funds had been deposited to the Grand
Treasurer's reservoir account.
The Crocker-Anglo National Bank of San Francisco receives all
income from investments under a custodial arrangement (periodically
amended and revdsed) which has been in existance between the Grand
Lodge and the Bank's predecessor since April 1. 1920. Such receipts,
together with collections on notes, proceeds of sales and other items
transmitted directly to the Bank, are deposited by it in the account
for the particular fund involved.
This custodial arrangement or agreement also covers securities owned
by the several accounts of Grand Lodge and which securitdes may be
withdrawn from such depository only in accordance with Section 146 of
the "California Masonic Code."

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

101

For purposes of routine operation, money is transferred from the
main accounts carried by the Grand Treasurer to "Operating Accounts"
maintained under different signature arrangements. Appropriations and
other special items such as those covering capital expenditures, and
which merit special handling, are paid by checks drawn by the Grand
Treasurer on the appropriate account.
The magnitude of these transactions is indicated by the figures of
total mcome and disbursements tabulated in the auditor's reports, and
as herein summarized.

The above recap of our income and disbursements is given in brief
to invite sufficient interest for you to review the auditor's reports in
detail. As officers of your respective lodges, it is your responsibility-a
part of the job.

chasing power of the dollar has been declining all too rapidly during the
past 25 years, and, if we are honest with ourselves, we must recognize
that fact. A financially strong lodge is usually strong in every other
respect; so, too, our Grand Lodge. By conducting our affairs on a
businesslike basis, following sound business principles, we, too, shall
remain strong and worthy of the name of Masonry.
My second recommendation then is directed to the attention of the
officers of the constituent lodges, particularly those lodges whose financial stature has failed to provide reasonable growth due to an inadequate
dues structure. Take a careful look at your particular situation. For
the officers to delay in recommending an increase in dues is only natural.
We must, however, be realistic and face the facts. With built-in
automatic pay increases in long-term labor contracts, the continued
policy of spending borrowed money at all levels of our economy, the
value of the dollar must, of necessity, continue to decline. In calling th.is
problem to your attention, I want to issue a word of caution. In determining what constitutes a proper dues and initiation fee structure for a
Masonic lodge, keep in mind that under no circumstances should they
be placed at an amount where Masonry ceases to have an universal
appeal. Ability to pay should never be made the test for membership. T 0
paraphrase--the high and the low, the rich and the poor, should all be
able to. unite and ca~se true friendship to exist among those who might
otherw1se have remained at a perpetual distance. You, as officers, have
been e.lected to display real leadership for your lodges-a leadership
that will keep your lodge ever alert and capable of handling every financial adversity or requirement.

104

COMMENTS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

Before closing this report there are two other matters relating to
finance which I feel impelled to bring to your attention.
I am sure we are all in agreement that the success of a Masonic
lodge or Grand Lodge is not measured by its financial strength or stability even though financial strength and reserves against adverse times
are highly desirable. This Grand Lodge is now assembled for its 109th
Annual Communication. True, the Masonic Homes Endowment fund is
a sizeable fund, but when we delete from the figures the monies belonging
to the Endowment Fund, the California Masonic Memorial Temple, the
Homes and other Special Funds, the Grand Lodge of California Pree
and Accepted Masons had total assets at the close of the fiscal year
June 30, 1958, of $732,996.18. This represents an average net gain of
less than $7,000 per year for the first 108 years of our existence. Certainly this is not in keeping with the dignity and high purpose of the
Grand Lodge. In these days of inflation and reasonably good times we
should have a program of continuing financial growth. Sound business
principles would dictate such a policy.
It is my recommendation to this Grand Lodge that we include in our
Grand Lodge annual budget some portion of our per capi.t a for the
definite purpose of building a surplus to be added to the capital assets
of this Grand Lodge.
My final thought in this report deals with the dues structure of the
constituent lodges. Of course, the Grand Lodge is only as strong
financially and spiritually as are the constituent lodges. It was in the
year 1948 that the minimum dues for constituent lodges was raised from
$9.00 to $12.00 per annum. As the result of that legislation 207 lodges
were called upon to raise their dues to the new minimum. At that time,
out of 594 lodges in existence, 337 were then at $12.00. At the close of
the fiscal year June 30, 1957, we had 677 constituent lodges. Of this
group 320 still hold to the minimum dues structure of $12.00 per year.
Out of these 320 lodges, 146 lodges were a part of those 207 lodges
called upon to raise their dues in 1948 from $9.00 per year to $12.00
per year.
In his 1957 Annual Report, Brother Lloyd E. Wilson, Grand
Secretary, presented some rather interesting figures in this regard. I
commend them for your review and study. I have no intention of
recommending that G.rand Lodge again increase the minimum dues for
constituent lodges, certainly not at this time. This should be a determination by the individual lodge. The fact remains, however, that the pur-

REPORT OF GRAND LECTURER
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This is my sixth annual report, covering the activities of the Grand
Lecturer and those of the Committee on Ritual.
The usual Spring Conferences of Inspectors were held as follows:
Divisions 1 and 2, at Bijou, Lake Tahoe, June 20-22, 1958, conducted jointly by Worshipful Clare B. Campbell and Worshipful Ralph
M. Foote, Assistant Grand Lecturers.
Division 3, at Guerneville, May 16-18, 1958, conducted by Worshipful Arthur J. Kahn, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 4, at Yosemite, June 6-8, 1958, conducted by Worshipful
Raymond G. Taylor, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 5, at Ventura, April 18-20, 1958, conducted by Worshipful
Donald G. Campbell, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
Division 6, at Garden Grove, March 21-23, 1958, conducted by
Worshipful W. Ben Sorrells, Assistant Grand Lecturer.
At each of these conferences the work was fully and well done by
the Inspectors of the respective division. These Conferences are, in
my opinion, an important factor in maintaining the uniformity and
excellence of our ritual.
At each of the Conferences, the Inspectors were addressed by the
Grand Master, and at two of them by the Grand Secretary as well, on
matters of interest and importance to the Inspectors.
At some of these Conferences, meetings of the Ritual Committee
were held to consider various matters pertaining to the ritual. A special
meeting of the Committee was also held at San Francisco, on November
30 and December 1, 1957, with all members of the Committee present,
at which meeting the entire work of the three degrees was reviewed and
performed by the Assistant Grand Lecturers.
The annual reports received by me from the Inspectors of the
jurisdiction, as required by Section 161 of the California Masonic Code,
show that most of our lodges are in good working condition and that
most of them are actively at work. As usual, however, some matters
have been disclosed by the reports which require attention, and they will
be referred to the Inspectors for their attention and correction.
As I have reported in previous years, the Committee has no suggestions whatever for any changes in the esoteric work.
With the approval of the Grand Master, I made a trip to Honolulu
and the outer Islands, and there conducted schools of instruction, as well
as rehearsals for the Dedication and Constitution ceremonies for Lodge
Maui No. 472 and the new Waikiki Lodge No. 774. A·I together I spent
well over flfty hours in instruction, rehearsals and participation in the
ceremonies which were conducted by the Grand Master. As to the
ritual in the lodges in the Islands, it is my firm conviction that it will take

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

107

more than intermittent trips to bring their ritual up to the required
standard, and it is my recommendation that an Assistant Grand Lecturer
should be sent there each year to give the required instruction to these
brethren and to assist the Inspectors.
This appears to be the desire of the Inspectors as well as the officers
of the Island lodges. They are certainly entitled to the same ritual
instruction as are the mainland brethren.
In closing, may I express to the Grand Master my personal thanks
for his many courtesies during the past year, and to the Grand Secretary
and Assistant Grand Secretary my appreciation for their ever-ready
assistance; and my thanks to you brethren for the opportunity of serving
you.
Respectfully submitted,
ELBERT W. DAVIS, Grand Lecturer

ANNUAL REPORT OF
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD
Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board submits herewith for your
consideration, its 26th Annual Report, covering the period of July 1.
1957 to June 30, 1958. This report brings to a close another fiscal year
in which the brethren of this Jurisdiction have again demonstrated that
"Masons Take Care of Their Own," not only during the fleeting present
but for generations to come.
CONTRIBUTIONS THROUGH LoDGES

This past year, 81,686 brethren contributed $421,633.62 to the
Homes Endowment Fund, a permanent tribute and lasting example of
their Masonic love and affection. This is an all-time high, and an increase
of $49,500 above the contributions of a year ago. These figures are for
contributions through the lodges only, and do not include special gifts
and bequests. The contributions of this year brought the total of the
Endowment Fund to $8,163,258.55. This amount may seem large at
first glance. However, the income from the Fund still amounts to less
than half the expenses of operating the Homes and those expenses, like
all others, continue to increase each year. During the year just past, the
operating expenses of the Homes were $715,673.00 and the income from
the Endowment was $313,658.00. It is self-evident that a much greater
Endowment is needed and our job is not complete.
WILLS AND BEQUESTS

In addition to the contributions through the lodges, $78,913.77 was
contributed to the Endowment through Bequests, the final expression of
love from those-who have been called from labor in this life. To make a
bequest to the Endowment, this lasting Monument of Masonry, is truly
"leaving foot-prints in the sands of time." Wills and Bequests are becoming an increasingly important activity of the Endowment Board and
we hope the lodges will give further considered thought to the potential
of this phase of our Endowment program. A new pamphlet, on this
subject exclusively, entitled "Wills and Bequests," has recently been
prepared by brother Everett Houser, Chairman of the Research Committee of Grand Lodge and is now available to the lodges, through the
Endowment Board.
We hope every lodge will order a supply of these pamphlets and
send one to each member, to the end that many more Masons might remember the Masonic Homes Endowment in their Will.
HONOR ROLL LODGl~S

This year 365 lodges achieved the Honor Roll by contributing an
average of at least $2.00 per member. This is a net increase of 80 lodges
on the Honor Roll above the previous year. Many outstanding records
were established, as a careful study of the figures from individual lodges.
found elsewhere in this report, will disclose. The experience of many of

purpose.

PERCENTAGE OF CONTRIBUTORS

You will note in this year's report that the "percentage of members
contributing" is shown for each lodge, for the first time, in addition to
the dollar amount. A careful analysis of those figures should prove interesting. The amount of $421,598.22 this year was contributed by approximately 35% of the members of the Jurisdiction and 65% of the
members made no contribution to the Endowment Fund. In fact, 75 of
the 365 lodges attaining the Honor Roll this year did so with less than
35% of their members contributing. Our great aim and fond hope is
that more and more of the 65 % will soon experience the joy and satisfaction of making an annual contribution and their sharing in this most
worthy cause.

Grand Secretary, M.W. Lloyd E. Wilson: the Assistant Grand Secretary. Brother Henry D. Oliphant, and all members of their staff, who
have been extremely cooperative and helpful to the Members of this
Board in general. and to its Chairman in particular; to the Grand Treasurer, M .W. Edward H. Siems. the trusted custodian of our funds; to the
Masters, Wardens and lodge Endowment Committeemen. who have devoted much time and work on behalf of the Endowment: to the lodge
Seuetaries, who in most cases had the job of mailing out the printed
items to members, as well as receiving. handling and issuing receipts for
contributions, and we know in many lodges the Secretary is the perennial
guiding light for the Endowment program in his lodge: to the Inspectors,
who have cooperated so wonderfully well and assisted so greatly in the
Endowment work. In many cases the officers of a lodge have been enthused to place their lodge on the Honor Roll because the Inspector expressed or evidenced a real interest in the Endowment: and to all officers

GRANO LODGE OF CALIPORNIA

REPORT OF COMMITTE E ON COMMERCI ALISM

better than to quote from a portion of his letter which was sent to the
Pharaoh of the Supreme Pyramid Ancient Order of Sciots, under date
of April 7, 1958. We quote as follows:
"With three direct violations of our law in one area alone it is only
natural to assume that the same violations are occurring all over the
State. This not only causes confusion and difficulties within the fraternity, but activities such as these certainly do not bring credit to our
fraternity.
"On the basis of the information before me I am inclined to take
drastic action if necessary, and if there are any more reports of similar
activities by the Pyramid s in California I will be inclined to issue an
Edict prohibiting Masons in the California Jurisdiction from belonging
to or having any part in the activities of the Sciots.
"For your own protection and in the best interests of the Sciots. I
would s u ~rnest that an official order be issued to all of the Pyramids in
the C a lifornia Jurisdiction calling their attention to the laws which
govern Masonic activities in this jurisdiction and directing that there be
no such affairs or activities in the future. I would suggest that this order
point out that Masonic law should be observed in spirit as well as in
fact and that attempts to circumvent the law will only bring difficulties
to the Sciots."
At the time of writing this report no further violations have been
brought to the attention of your committee. It can only be hoped that the
Sciots too will recognize and remember that they are Masons first and
that they owe a definite allegiance to their own lodges and to this
Grand Lodge.
(Since this report was written we are in formed by the Grand Master
that he met with the Pharaoh of the Supreme Pyramid of the Sciots
subsequent to his above-written letter. He explained our rules and
regulations: the reasons for them. and generally discussed our relationship with the Sciots organization. The Grand Master was assured that
the Sciots would make a special effort to see that there were no further
violations of our law among their various Pyramids. It is to be hoped
that the assurance thus given the Grand Master will be fulfilled.)

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Commercialism is most happy to report that the
reported violations of our law during the past year have been less than
during any preceding year. This is no doubt due to the continuing educational program which has been a consistent part of our work. In
addition, our Grand Master has given generously of his time to meet
with various organizations and groups requiring Masonic membership,
affiliation or sponsorship, and to discuss and clarify our law as it may
pertain to them. His great patience, wisdom. courage and leadership
has done much to bring about better understanding and cooperation
among these organizations and groups. It is to be hoped that the supremacy of this Grand Lodge definitely established last year, and bulwarked
this year by rulings of our Grand Master. w ill not again be challenged.
SHRINE

We reported last year that the cooperation we had received from the
various Shrine Temples had been excellent . We are happy to report
that this cooperation has continued. In the very few instances of reported
violations, generally among Shrine Clubs. a conference with the Potentate of the Shrine having jurisdiction of such Club has brought quick
correction of such violations. Your committee wishes to acknowledge
this attitude on the part of the Potentates and we trust that the cordial
relationships which have existed this year will continue with potentates
of the future.
SCIOTS

Reports were received concerning certain activities of this prerequisite organization . particularly with reference to Pyramids in San
Diego County. Investigation disclosed that a raffle and Hobo Dance was
held for the purpose of rais ing funds for an organization within a
Pyramid. At the Hobo Dance refreshment tickets were sold at the
rate of I 0 for $1.00. which were honored at the rate of three tickets for
one beer. Investigation also showed that this particular Pyramid held
its meetings in a certain hall and regularly served beer before and after
the meeting.
Another Pyramid held a public installation at a certain club where
liquor was sold at two bars. Refreshment tickets were sold three for
$1.00, which were honored at either of the two bars for spiritous drinks
of the purchaser's choice.
Still another Pyramid held an open installation where full bar facilities were set up in the rear of the East. Drinks of all kinds were sold
for cash. During the installation ceremonies persons along the sidelines
had drinks in their hands and one officer had a drink sitting on his
station pedestal. The officers to be installed entered the hall to the tune
of "The Beer Barrel Polka."
A report of these and other activities was made to the Grand M aster
and his reaction was forthright, firm and to the point. We can do no

1

ROYAL ORDER OF CARITAS AND AMARANTH FOUNDATION, IN C.

At our last com munication an Edict of our then Grand Master, Most
Worshipful L. Harold Anderson, prohibiting all Masons subject to the
jurisdiction of California from being, becoming or remaining a member
of the Royal Order of Caritas or of the Amaranth Foundation, Inc., or
their successors by change of name, or for any such Mason to aid or
assist, directly or indirectly, said Order of Caritas or said Amaranth
Foundation, Inc., or their successors by change of name, in any manner
whatsoever, was approved and made a permanent Edict of Grand Lodge.
We regret to report to you that a number of our brethren apparently
thought more of such organizations than of their obligations to Masonry
and continued their membership in and support of such organizations.

124

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

As a result four Masonic trials have been conducted and in each instance
the respective individuals have been found guilty of the charges preferred
against them and guilty of un-Masonic conduct. Investigation is being
made of other brethren who have been reported to your committee as
being members of and giving support to these organizations.
Reports were also received by your committee that various Temple
Associations and lodges were renting space in Masonic T em pies to the
Royal Order of Caritas for their meetings and other activities. A report
was made to our Grand Master and under date of February I 0, 1958,
he issued a directive to all of our lodges in which he s tated:
" .. . The renting of space to this group or assisting them to hold
meetings is in direct violation of the Edict and should not be done. I
have not directed that any action be taken against those who have in
this manner violated the Edict. but I am advising you of the situation so
that there will be no violations in the future."
PUBLICATIONS

At our 1954 Annual Communication a resolution was adopted which
authorized the Grand Master "to institute actions in the courts of
California on behalf of the Grand Lodge, F . & A. M . of the State of
California. to establish that its name and the words. Mason . Freemason .
Free and Accepted Mason, Masonry and Masonic and Masonic symbols
and emblems shall not be used for fraudulent purposes or for private
gain or profit ..."
Purs uant to that resolution M . · .W. ·.Henry C . Clausen , Past Grand
M aster and Judge Advocate. instituted four suits in the Superior Court
of California against four so-called Masonic publications. One publication. The Masonic News, published in Southern California, folded
without the necessity of trial. A trial was had in the case of the
Masonic World Publishing Company and its owner and a decision was
rendered in our favor. In April of this year the two remaining suits
against the Masonic Trestleboard and the Masonic Star were tried and
decisions rendered in our favor and permanent injunctions issued. Great
credit should be given our Judge Advocate, Past Grand Master Henrv
·
C. Clausen for the success we have achieved in these matters.
Another publication, the Masonic Review Diges t. made its appearance in Southern California during the past year. Your chairman was
successful in getting a conference w ith the owner. When our law was
explained to him . and also the results of our legal actions ins tituted
against other publications, he agreed to cease operations entirely. No
further editions of the publication have been published and we sincerely
believe that none will.
It thus appears that this troublesome matter has now been pretty
well resolved. With continued education of the Craft and prerequisite
bodies we feel that the work of the committee in this field should be
greatly reduced.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

125

REGULATIONS

Your committee has, for the past several months, given consideration
to the preparation of rules and regulations setting forth the requirements
of our law relative to matters which govern our lodges and prerequisite
organizations and groups and which generally come under the scrutiny
of or are referred to this committee. The Grand Master was consulted
and he authorized us to proceed. The result has been the preparation
of such rules and regulations which, after revision and review. have
been approved by the Grand Master, and have been or will be sent to
all Lodges, Temples and Associations and, we hope. to prerequisite
organizations and groups. We feel that the work of this committee
can be greatly reduced if all concerned will carefully study these rules
and regulations and then see that they are followed. A copy of such
rules and regulations is attached to this report. (Exhibit A.)
MISCELLANEOUS

Various reports have been received of activities of clubs and individuals which have constituted violations of our law. No attempt is here
made to list them all. In all instances a letter or conference has brought
quick compliance and expressions of regret. It is our sincere conviction
that a continuing educational program is required and we solicit the aid
and support of the Masters and Inspectors in such a program .
CON CLUSION

The report of this committee would not be complete without an
expression of our appreciation to the Grand Master for the time which
he has so generously given to us. The nature of our work is such that
we must constantly confer with him , either personally or through correspondence, as he is the one who must set the policy and make the
rulings and decisions on matters which are referred to us. Whenever
possible, he has endeavored to "whisper good counsel" and seek coopera tion, but always with such firmness that none can or could doubt
his love for our Fraternity and his determination to see that its laws.
ordinances, rules and regulations were strictly adhered to. To work
with him has not only been a pleasure but has enriched our Masonic life
and education.
Respectfully submitted,
RALPH K. PIERSON, Chairman .
WILLARD BRAASCH
HERBERT R. HARGRAVE

EXHIBIT A
REGULATIONS GOVERNING ORGANIZATIONS SUBJECT TO THE JURISDICTION
oP THE MosT WoRSHIPPUL GRAND LoocE. F. & A. M. oF CALIFORNIA

The following regulations are posted to preclude violations as set

126

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

forth in the California Masonic Code by organizations subject to the
jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of
California, by reason of requiring Masonic membership, affiliation or
sponsorship.
The term "organization" as herein used is defined to include:
(a) Any subordinate lodge;
( b) Any group, chapter, order. club. association or organization
requiring Masonic affiliation or sponsorship, including but not
limited to:
York Rite Bodies
Scottish Rite Bodies
Shrine
Shrine Clubs
Scio ts
Grotto
Eastern Star
Order of Amaranth
White Shrine of Jerusalem
Social Order of Beauceant
Job's Daughters
Rainbow Girls
De Molay
Masonic Clubs
These regulations apply to all Master Masons living within the
jurisdiction of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of
California, irrespective of whether such Master Mason is a member of
a lodge in California or elsewhere.
REGULATIONS

1. ADVERTISING
No organization as herein defined nor any member thereof shall
solicit or accept advertising of any kind for publication or insertion in
any roster, program. bulletin or announcements to be printed or published claiming to be Masonic in name or character.
No such organization or any member thereof shall sponsor. insert.
place or print advertising of any kind in any publication claiming to be
Masonic in name or character. ( C.M.C. 334).
This regulation does not prohibit the placement in bonafide newspapers of legitimate news items of organization , group or club activities
or advertisements in said newspapers in connection with rummage sales
which do not use the name of any of the organizations hereinbefore
named or any group thereof.
2. PUBLIC SUPPORT
No organization as herein defined nor any agency thereof such as

127

social clubs , mothers' clubs, sewing circles or other clubs or groups within
such organization, nor any member thereof. usin g any name whatever
shall sponsor any event, project. scheme or plan wherein public support
is requested or solicited on behalf of such organization or any agency or
group thereof. Tickets or other items may not be sold to the general
public. (C.M.C. 33 ). Rummage sales wherein public support is
solicited in the name of the organization or of any group thereof are
forbidden.
This regulation does not prohibit the sale of tickets to members, their
families or friends, for breakfasts. dinners, card parties, dances, bazaars.
and so forth, nor to events, their entire proceeds of which go to a recognized charity of the fraternity or o rgan ization.
3. SoLICITATION OF GIFTS
The solicitation of merchants, firms, business houses, or the public
for gifts of merchandise, money or prizes of any kind for or in connection with the general activities of the group or organization, such as
dinners, parties , and meetings, is strictly forbidden. This regulation
does not prohibit a member of any organization from voluntarily donating such a gift or contributing to a charity.

5. COMMERCIAL VENTURES
No organization herein defined or any agency or group thereof shall
directly or indirectly engage in any business, pro ject, venture, promotion ,
scheme or plan which is unethical, misleading, fraudulent or illegal. No
such organization shall knowingly receive money or property a s a donation or contribution from such operations. ( C.M.C. 332).

5. GAMBLING
No organization as herein defined nor any member or group of
members thereof' shall directly or indirectly give aid or countenance to
any raffle. lottery, or other gambling enterprise or accept any of the
proceeds or profits therefrom. (C.M.C. 685).
Door prizes are permissible only if those attending do not pay
anything of value for the chance to receive the door prize. In this con nection the payment of the usual charge of the restaurant or organization serving a d in ner, lunch, or breakfast is not the payment of something
of value for th e privilege of drawing and the door prizes must be of
nominal value, such as candy, and may be dona ted by members of th e
organization.
Table or score prizes at card parties may be given if the prizes are
donated by the members and are of nominal value such as can dy.
In case of doubt or disagreement as to the applicability of these regu lations to any particular event or enterprise, consultation should be had
with the Inspector of the District.
Attest:
Approved
LLOYD E. WILSON ,

LEO E. ANDERSON,

Grand Secretary
Grand Master of Masons in California.

GRAND ORATION
MELVIN A. PIXLEY, Grand Orator
September 30. 1958

Most Worshipful, Grand Lodge Officers, Past Grand Masters.
Distinguished Guests, Members of Grand Lodge. and Brethren:
If protocol permitted Grand Orations to be dedicated, then the
following address should be dedicated to the person who not only
al lowed it to be given, but of greater importance, who has inspired his
fellow Craftsmen throughout the year, just as this edifice will inspire
future generations.
o~ Grand Master has not only WISDOM and STRENGTH, but possesses and displays the BEAUTY of HUMILITY.
To you, Most Worshipful, and the other Grand Lodge Offic~rs. 1_11Y
personal thanks and appreciation for your many kindnesses which ins pired this address entitled
PROPER COMMUNICATIONS-THE ANSWER
We read in the Holy Writings that it was decreed in the wisdom
and counsels of Diety aforetime that a house should be built, erected
to God and dedicated to H is Holy Name. This structure was erected
and known a s King Solomon's Temple. perhaps the most wonderful
structure in the world's history.
The early architects and the architecture found in King Solomo~'s
Temple communicated to future generations the thoughts. needs, pnde
and glory of the earliest races. and their reverence for the. gr~at
Creator. Their designs still inspire and are the objects of adm1rat1on
now found in the Masonic theme.
Now we also read in the past Annual Communications of this
Grand Lodge that it was decreed in the wisdom and by the foresight
of the Masters. Wardens and Past Masters that this Gra nd Lodge
build a Temple to communicate to the world that California Freemasons, honoring their heroic dead. erect a Temple, dedicated to Freemasonry, virtue, and a universal benevolence, that the cause of fre~­
dom for which they died shall ever be therein the sacred trust of their
Brethren and of Freemasons yet unborn.
It is interesting to note that after the Great Fire of 1906 here in
San Francisco, there was left standing here on the site of our new
Temple three columns. These same columns today stand in Golden
Gate Park, bearing the prophetic motto "The Portals of the Past Will

Be the Gateway to the Future."
To carry out that prophesy this new Temple has been here erected
to the glory of God. bearing symbols of the past in memory of those

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

129

who are gone. and opening a new gateway to the future service of
humanity and the advancement of Freemasonry in California.
The modern architects and the architecture found in the California
Masonic Memorial Temple will communicate to future generations not
only the progress of Masonry in California, fully recognizing the
industry of the past and present, hardships and toils, bravery and
valor, but the accomplishment of carrying out two Masonic lessons
of Faith and Work by emphasizing love of freedom and proving that
we assumed our responsibilities.
Words are indeed an imperfect vehicle for the translation of human emotion especially when that emotion is centered around the
memory of those who were but are not. Words certainly cannot
properly describe the accomplis hments of those who have made pos~
sible this very occasion, achieving their purpose in maintaining for
us and for Freemasons yet unborn our great heritage-Freedom.
Time will not suffice for a detailed report or inventory of all Masonic structures, symbols or words that communicate. but at this
communication and following the dedicatory ceremonies. it is important as a matter appertaining to the Craft. to pause and concentrate
on the value and needs of proper communications, especially those
that radiate from Operative and Speculative Masonry.
Before our present means of communication symbols were used
and understood by both the educated and uneducated. Today some
people consider symbols to be old fashioned, fanciful. or even an
expression of superstition. These people forget that there was a time
when education was not as widespread as it is today, and in those
days certain objects and numbers were used to indicate certain lessons or ideals to people in general. Symbols were indeed the very
objective of the human family, directing life along its wonderful
course from the cradle of the races in the Far East to today's civilization, just as today Masonic symbols, illuminated by Masonic light
and divine rays, enable us to communicate to the initiated knowledge
and wisdom . that which to the profane remains as darkness and
ignorance.
The most common communicative symbols known to man are
those given to us by God a nd are the symbols normally classed as
nature, for by the use of the fiv e common senses, hearing. seeing, feeling . smelling and tasting. we are not only protected but enjoy the
beauty and love of the Supreme Architect. Throughout this masterful plan we constantly receive the communication of the perfect balance and harmony created and intended for life.
Do not the following symbols bring to our minds past experiences?
Beautiful as the clouds may be, how many times have they indicated
to us that a storm is approaching? Think of the beautiful flowers
with their fragrance and delicate colors, communicating their many
symbolic meanings. Carvings and statutes, such as those found on

130

PROCEEDINGS OF THF.

the very walls of this Temple. which inspire the receptive mind.
Photography. some pictures reflecting to us happy occasions . and
others of sorrow. Murals. like those presented by this Grand Lodge
which are now seen in the Washington Memorial Temple. one depicting the Father of our Country and his officers attending church for
the purpose of raising funds to alleviate suffering among the poor.
The other, President Washington receiving the silver plate which is
deposited in the cornerstone of the United States Capitol. these communicate to us, as does this structure. our belief in charity and
freedom.
Think of the many kinds of lights. not only those which beautify
the heavens but those found in our lodges and in our homes. Yet.
there are those which control our physical movements on the streets
and walks of life.
Do not the rays of the morning sunburst convey to us that "This
day is mine, yesterday it was God's, tomorrow it will be his again
and our acts will be recorded in eternity". There are communicative
rituals which are expressed by robes. words and movements. There
are the blessings communicated by rest, and a symbolic reminder of
this is in the six windows at the top of this very structure. for "in
six days God created the Hea [)ens and the Earth. and rested upon
the seventh".
Modern transportation such as ships. trains. automobiles, trucks
and airplanes communicate departure or arrival of our loved ones
and the security and relief which they might bring. not to overlook
the symbolic meaning of the destruction and devastation of war
which they can create. laying waste and destroying many valuable
monuments of antiquity on which the utmost exertions of human
genius we re employed.
Then there is that which is quietly communicated by the touch
of a loved one's hand upon our brow; and one can never forget
those childhood memories of the fragrance of our Mother's delicacies communirnting to us the pleasure we were about to experience.
There a re illuminated billboards. arranged in such a manner as
to influence our lives. and visible signs of all descriptions. lighted
and unlighted . to direct our way. The cross conveys that a church
exists. even the direction of an arrow. without much question to
our minds. indicates the route we are to follow .
How important has it been in our lives when a s mile or a cheery
greeting of "good morning" from a friend , or even a stranger, has
helped our day.
Many times two symbols when taken together have an entirely
different meaning. One of the best known examples to us is the
Square and Compass placed on the Holy Bible.
There are many other forms of communication. For many years
man has known that words a re merely man-made sounds which

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

131

indicate things, places or items. and since their use came into being
many phases o f symbolism or sign language have been discontinued.
But by the progress of using merely man-made sounds. the pooling and
advancement of knowledge has taken place. Instead of remaining
helpless because of the limitations of our own experiences and knowledge. instead of having to discover what others have already explored,
repeating their errors. we can go on from where others left off to
greater accomplishments. All that is needed by men (or Masons ) is
man's ability to cooperate.
The invention of writing was a tremendous step forward fo r
mankind . The accuracy of reports can be checked and rechecked
by successive generations. and knowledge is not restricted to memory or symbols. Writing resulted in progress and development,
actually opening the doors to modern education and public schools.
a landmark in our progress which Masons will defend as a part of
our freedom. Thus we trace the histor y and development of the
basic means of communication. What we do with these methods of
communication will greatly determine our future and the future of
mankind .
Words. their proper meaning, the way they are spoken and written today control our thoughts and , my brethren, "a man's life is what
his thoughts make of it." "What you are is what God gives you."
Most surely. what you become. in the final analysis. is what you give
God.
Man's future progress and accomplishments will be governed by
words, symbols. or a combination of both. Yet how vital and important it is that we avoid the danger of worshipping the symbols
or rituals rather than that which they represent. The Masonic pin
is not to inform the world that one is a Mason . but rather a remi nder
to oneself of our duty and responsibilities.
The modern use of mathematics and chemistry signs, coupled
with words. greatly assisted in breaking the atom. Present-day traveling is controlled by words and symbols; even maps are a combination of the two which communicates to us the correct direction. If
maps are improperly prepared and are incorrect. actually no harm
befalls us until we attempt to use them and then we discover we are
traveling the wrong road. This philosophy challenges all men and

The annual audit for the fiscal year ending June 30, 1958 indicates
a deficit of $54,675.15 before profit from sale of investments or a net
deficit of $37,H3.95 after this item.
While it appears that we may have a continuing deficit for some

increased Endowment Fund income will solve most of our problems.

PROPOSED

NEW HOSPITAL FACILITIES AT THE
MASONIC HoME, DECoTo

· At present there are three hundred fifty men and women in the Decoto Home, eighty of whom are bed cases. This taxes the capacity of
present facilities, and it has become necessary to expand to properly
care for the aged. The average age of the people in the Home is 82 years,
and the average age of the bed cases is 90 years. The facilities for bed
cases must be increased.
The maintenance and operation of a Home such as the Masonic

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

140

141

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

Home at Decato is subject to license and regulation by the State of
California. The buildings must meet certain standards of construction,
comply with the California Uniform Building Code, the Rules and Regulations of the Fire Marshal, Industrial Accident Commission, and the
California Department of Public Health. The Regulations for ambulatory cases living in the Home are under the direction of the State Bureau
of Hospitals of the Department of Public Health. Obviously the latter
regulations are more exacting and severe.
There have been recent changes in codes to improve health and
safety conditions for the ill and aged. In many instances these changes
affect existing facilities and are mandatory, particularly in hospital facilities. In considering the needed expansion at the Home, it is more
logical to build a new modern independent unit which will comply with
all State requirements for care of the bed cases rather than remodel existing facilities to comply with present codes. This will then release
eighty additional beds for ambulatory cases for which the codes are not
as strict. The proposed new unit, designed for 131 beds, will allow for
approximately 50 additional beds beyond the present bare requirements.
The selection of the site for the new unit has received considerable
consideration. Inasmuch as this is an expansion of the existing facilities,
it must relate to these facilities. Therefore, it was located adjacent to the
nurses' home, the kitchen and parking area, and directly accessible from
the main building by means of a bridge. The site is steep, but advantage
was taken of this by providing accessible terraces for all floors except
the fourth floor. The nurses' home, the kitchen, and other existing facilities are adequate for this increase in the plant and for the present it
is economical to expand the existing facilities. In the future due to site
limitations and limitations of some facilities it will be necessary to consider another completely new and related group of buildings on a new
site on the existing property or elsewhere.
The new unit is a four-story and basement reinforced concrete structure containing 62 two-bed wards and 7 single rooms. A hospital elevator
serves all floors from the basement to the fourth floor. Access is available
from the basement level for food carts and deliveries. The main entrance
to the building is at street level on the first floor. The nurses' entrance is
on the second floor opposite the nurses' home, and an enclosed connecting bridge provides a connecting corridor from the second floor to the
existing main building.
The basement contains service rooms consisting of a large mechanical equipment room, morgue, linens and clothes storage, general storage,
soiled linen, a rinse and dry laundry, and a garbage room. The basement
floor is at the same elevation as the existing kitchen across the street and
in fair weather food carts can cross the street and be taken up the elevator to the diet kitchen.
The first floor with its main entrance lobby is accessible from the

street by a slight ramp. In addition to the lobby. nurses' lounge, and
locker room, this floor contains a clinic, examination and trea~ment
rooms, and a number of two-bed wards with the necessary nurses station, baths and utilities. The wards open onto a terrace.
The second floor has a diet kitchen which serves this entire new unit
in addition to the two-bed wards, private rooms, and the necessary
utility rooms. The food carts come up to this floor by way. o~ the el~v~tor
or, in inclement weather, across the bridge from the existmg building.
The food is served in the diet kitchen and the trays distributed to the
various rooms throughout the building. Toast and other minor items on
the menu will be prepared in this diet kitchen. On this floor, some wards
open onto a terrace, and others onto balconies.
The third and fourth floors have two-bed wards and private rooms
besides the necessary nurses' station, baths and utilities. Those on the
third floor open either onto a terrace or onto balconies, and those on the
fourth floor open onto balconies. The roof in addition to the elevator
penthouse has space for fans and a cooling tower.
Each typical two-bed ward has a sliding glass door and screen to
either a four and a half foot wide balcony or an open terrace for use by
the occupants in wheel chairs when the weather is favorable. There is a
small storage cabinet in each ward for the personal eff~cts of each occupant, a lavatory and one connecting toilet for each pair of wards .. Each
ward and room has forced ventilation with all air heating and coohng on
thermostatic controls.
Floor finish will be vinyl asbestos, except for certain rooms which will
have ceramic tile. Examination and treatment rooms will have floors required by law.
Medical care for the institution is provided by a clinic and hospital
at some distance. At present, cases requiring surgery are transferred to
this hospital. Doctors visit the Home at reg?lar interv~ls or by .call: In
this new unit, space is provided for doctors consultation, exammation,
treatment, and minor surgery. It has all the necessary facilities such as
doctors' dressing space, scrub-up, sterilizers, and clean-up. S~a~e is also
provided. for a cast room with a portable X-ray, a dental chmc, and a
small clinical laboratory., W~!le compact, this medical treatment and
surgery unit will be quite complete.
The present transformer and main switchboard for the en!ire plant
are located on the site of the new building. A new vault and switchboard
room will be built at the rear court and terrace of the nurses' home at the
beginning of construction operations and the cut-over will be made with
the minimum of interruption of services.
A new fire alarm system will be installed extending through the entire home, which will substant.ially contribute to fire safety. With the

142

development planned, the areas presently used as hospital will be made
available for other uses which are now under consideration.
An estimate has been made of the cost of the complete construction
program which will provide new space for the care of one hundred and
thirty-one bed cases. This estimate approximates $1,000,000.00, which
does not include the furniture and equipment required. The plans have
received the approval of doctors expert in hospital administration and arrangement. as well as State Officials whose approval must necessarily be
obtained. The facility should serve Masonic Home at Decato adequately
for many years to come.
COVINA

In the progress of the children residing in our Covina Home, our
membership may be justly proud. Here, under the guidance of Superintendent Robert M. Henry and his very competent staff, sixty-seven children are beneficiaries of the kind care, love and protection of California
Masonry. That the opportunities afforded them are truly appreciated is
evident in their frequently voiced expressions of gratitude. For a review
of the home, school and community activities of the children, we commend to your attention the report of Superintendent Henry, which will
be included in the printed Proceedings.
To sustain the agricultural and 4-H programs, which have proven so
beneficial in developing leadership among the children, a farm building
program has been undertaken during the year, for the replacement of a
barn destroyed several years ago by fire, and several old wooden service
structures. It is expected that these new facilities will be completed and in
use at Covina before the end of the year.
Realizing that the leadership of our Superintendents is very vital to
the success of our two Homes, the Trustees are particularly gratified
that both Superintendent Henry and Superintendent David were this
year elected and installed as Worshipful Master by their respectful

REPORT OF SUPERINTENDENT-DECOTO HOME
To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
.
Brethren: It is my privilege and pleasure to present to you my third
annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Homes at Decato for
the year ending June 30, 1958.
The population of the Home on July 1. 1957 was 144 men and 212
women. The new members for the year consisted of 40 women, average
age being 77.58 years. and 31 men averaging 78.87 years of age. There
were 38 women, average age 84.43 years, and 33 men, average age of
83.60. who passed to the Celestial Lodge above during the year. Three
men were withdrawn from the Home during the year.
On June 30, 1958 we had a population of 353 members, consisting
of 139 men and 214 women, including 14 married couples. Two members
of the Home were united in marriage during the past year.

There are 80 patients confined in the hospital, with a capacity of 81.

seem most satisfied with this arrangement.

Sunday a month and on the other Sundays we have the services of ministers of other denominations in the area. To them we wish to extend
our thanks and appreciation for bringing their services to the Home for
the benefit of our members.
During the past year we obtained electrically heated food conveyors
for the hospital, which have been very satisfactory, as we are now able
to serve the patients h~t food, and it is much more appetizing.
We closed our Laundry on January I. 1958 and now send it out to
a commercial laundry in Oakland. The charges are proving satisfactory
and we. believe it will be more economical in the end.
Ne~ drapes were purchased for the dining room, which have made
it more attractive.
Many of the rooms and hallways were redecorated in various pastel
shades. The folks seem to enjoy the change in colors and it has done
much to raise their spirits.
Wark was started about two months ago in modernizing our boiler
plant and we will have two new boilers. The old boilers have been in
use some thirty-five to forty years. New underground pipes were installed, along with the rearrangement of some of the pipes in the
building. When this .work is completed, with the larger boilers. we

will enjoy a higher rate of efficiency, and less maintenance costs and
problems. They will be modem and automatic.
We have had the pleasure of witnessing Degrees in the Temple
being conferred by 19 various Lodges. Many other Lodges visited
the Home, some bringing with them a picnic lunch, also many programs were given in the Auditorium for the benefit of the members.
We sincerely appreciate their thoughtfulness of our members.
We also wish to extend our sincere thanks and gratitude to all the
various Lodges, Organizations, Associations and individuals who were
so thoughtful and generous with their entertaining programs, and all
the donations of books, magazines and other gifts. Also to the many
groups taking our members for the wonderful auto rides which they
have enjoyed so much.
Movies were supplied for each Thursday throughout the year by
MGM. Twentieth Century Fox, United Artists. Universal. Columbia,
RKO, and Warner Bros. booking companies. We are very grateful to
them for these movies which our people enjoyed every week.
It was an honor and privilege to welcome the Most Worshipful
Leo E. Anderson, Grand Master, on January 11, 1958. On this date
the Board of Trustees made their annual visitation to the Home and
held their quarterly meeting.
A reception was held in the Auditorium by the members of the
Home, in honor of the Grand Master and the members of the Board.
After their words of greeting, they were entertained by the members of
the Home with songs and a "Wedding Skit", after which refreshments were serv~d.
At different times during the year various Trustees visited the
Home, and it is always a privilege to welcome and assist them during
their inspections.
On August 17, 1957 the East Bay Past Matrons Association held
their annual reception for the Worthy Grand Matron. A luncheon
was held in the Basement Banquet Room, after which they adjourned
to the Auditorium for a reception in her honor.
We wish also to express our sincere thanks and appreciation to
this group for their splendid generosity, for 7,937 jars of jams and
jellies, 2,195 quarts of canned fruits and juices, along with other
items and $7.42 in cash.
We had a total of 4,778 visitors register and I know there were
many that did not register. These represented 382 Lodges in California, 35 foreign jurisdictions, including 4 foreign countries. Among
the dignitaries, there were two Grand Masters and two Past Grand
Masters. We appreciate all these Brethren visiting the Home and
hope they will come back again.

To the Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California:
It is with deep appreciation and a realization of the great privilege
which is mine to work with young people that I present to you my
tenth annual report as Superintendent of the Masonic Home for Children at Covina, for the year ending June 30, 1958.
HOME MEMBERSHIP

The population of our Masonic Home Family, as of June 30, 1958,
numbers sixty-seven children-thirty-nine boys and twenty-eight girls.
During the fiscal year of 1957-58, fifteen chrildren have been admitted to
the Home, six boys and nine girls. Fifteen children have departed from
the Home; one to enter the Service of his country in the United States
Army, nine to re-established homes, and five of our high school graduates. Two of these graduates are remaining at the Home and attending
Mount San Antonio Junior College. Graduate Sandra Larsen plans to
work at Disneyland this summer and to continue her education at Santa
Monica Junior College at the beginning of the fall term. Graduate Diann
Ostrander will be working at our Home this summer in our camp program and plans to attend Sawyer's Business College this fall. Another
graduate, Elinor Offinga, is completing her work at the Edgewood College of Beauty in Covina. Linda Allison graduated and received l.B.M.
training in Los Angeles. Larry Moody entered the Service and is with
the United States Air Force. Five boys and two girls were graduated
from Badillo Grammar School and will en·t er Covina High School at
the beginning of the fall term.

HEALTH AND WELFARE PROGRAM

We are able to report a good year for the children's health and welfare, due to the help and excellent supervision of Dr. W. P. Magan, Sr.,
and his Associates, and to the devotion and vigilance of our Home's
Nurse. We have had no serious health problem this past year, although
there have been the usual contagious diseases such as measles, chicken
pox, common cold, and Asiatic flu. In stressing preventive measures in
our health program, complete physical examinati ons are given at regular intervals during the year. We also continued vitamin supplemen ts
and polio immunization this year. The children's optometry and visual
needs are under the supervision of Drs. Johnston and McCormick. Dr.
Elmer King, an alumnus of the Covina Home, examines the children's
teeth periodically and administers the necessary care and treatment. The
orthodont ia program is administered by Dr. Teal of Covina. Seven
children have received orthodont ia treatment during this fiscal year.
There have been three tonsillectomies and one other minor surgery.
FARM AND MASONIC PIONEERS ' 4-H CLUB

A long-rang e plan of improvement of farm and grounds has been
progressin g, and within the coming year the completion of our Farm and
Service Buildings are in sight. These buildings and facilities replace
those destroyed by fire two years ago. The fish pond has been enlarged,
and two islands ~ave been formed in it; one to be used for future fishfries for the children, the other as a refuge and nesting place for the
Home's ducks and other water fowl. Recently, the pond was freshly
stocked with fish. Twenty-t wo of our children, seventeen boys and five
girls, are members of our Masonic Pioneers' 4-H Club. The Club has
received its Charter and Achievement Seal, a gold star, for the tenth
year. Maintaine d by the 4-H Club are a registered Hereford breeding
herd as well as fat stock, and a registered Duroc Jersey swine herd. The
Club produced in live weight, and the Home consumed, four thousand,
one hundred sixty-two pounds of beef and five thousand, nine hundred
and forty pounds of pork this past year.

ALUMNI OP THE CovINA HoME

Alumni Home-Coming Day last September was a happy day, very
well attended, with approximately five hundred alumni and their families
present. It is a most heartwarming experience to again meet with the
alumni who received much of their childhood training at our Home, to
hear of their marriages and the happy homes they have established, and
to find that the precepts of Masonic principles as taught in our Home
have helped them in their lives. The Covina Alumni Reunion is observed
on the second Sunday in September, and the Alumni Reunion Dinner in
San Francisco is on the Saturday preceding Grand Lodge. This past
year the Sacramento Alumni Picnic was on June 7. Invitations to these
reunions are mailed to every active alumnus, and encouragement is given
to each one to keep the Home informed of his present address. A copy of
the 1958 Masonic Home Newsletter was sent to all alumni, including
those in the Armed Services; to Masonic Lodges currently sponsoring a
child in the Home; and to Grand Lodge Officers.

TRIBUTE TO CHARLES ALBERT ADAMS
Myron E. Smith on behalf of the Trustees of the Masonic Homes
of California presented the following:
That great and original thinker, Emerson, said "Nothing great was
ever achieved without enthusiasm." Today, wise counselors tell us that
the ability to create enthusiasm in others is the quality above all others
which most distinguishes the executive and the leader.
How wonderful it is that California Masonry has been blest with a
leader whose enthusiasm has been a star in her crown for more than
half a century; whose leadership has lighted the course of Masonic
Homes of California for more than 40 years!
This great and good brother, who means so much to us, was born of
pioneer parents, Amos and Regina Adams, in the California "Mother
Lode" town of Mokelumne Hill, in Calaveras County. on November 25,
186 7-more than 90 years ago.
His father was the judge of the old Eleventh Judicial District, comprised of Amador, Calaveras and El Dorado Counties. In 1875 the
family moved to San Francisco, where our brother has ever since
resided, except for a short time in Oakland.
He received his education in the public schools of San Francisco and
Oakland, and in 1887, more than 70 years ago, was graduated from the
University of California's Hastings College of Law, and admitted to the
practice of the law.
Our brother has had a long and active professional. civic and fraternal life.
In the first World War, over the age at which he could be inducted
into military senlke. he was appointed associate director of Four-Minute
Men in California, and chairman of the Bureau of Speakers of the War
Savings Committee.
The devoted protagonist of public education, he was for several years
chairman of the section of education in the Commonwealth Club (and
of which he is still a member) and has been for many years a member
of the executive committee of the Public Education Society of San
Francisco. He is a former member of the State Board of Education and,
as chairman of its Text-Book Committee took a prominent part in the
controversy and subsequent litigations with reference to the adoption of
text books and which ultimately resulted in a decision by the Supreme
Court, which confirmed and definitely established the right of the State
Board to adopt such text books as were believed by its members to be
the best, even though they were not, and could not be. printed by the
State printer
A member of the Order of the Coif, he is today the oldest practicing
attorney in the City and County of San Francisco, and one of the
oldest active attorneys in the United States--honore d and respected as
one of the great leaders in his profession in his native Califomia.

His Masonic career has been an unusually long and active one--in
our Grand Lodge probably unique. because there has not been a year
since he entered Grand Lodge as Junior Warden of Excelsior Lodge
No. 166, in 1907, that he has not been either a member of an important
committee, or board, or an officer of Grand Lodge.
Before most of us were born, in 1901, he was initiated on May 8th,
passed on May 22nd and raised on May 29th in Excelsior Lodge No.
166-all in a span of three weeks, a feat in itself symbolic of his fabulous
memory. In 1908, he was elected Master of his lodge, and also appointed
to the Grand Lodge Committee on Finance.
In the years that have followed we have seen him serve the Grand
Lodge in countless capacities:
1908-Commit tee on Finance
1909--Special committee to recommend procedure to acquire good
title to San Gabriel property of the then Southern California
Masonic Home Association.

It has been said that to truly live is to live in the lives of others. The
brother whom we now honor is eight years older than the average age
( 82) of the residents at our Decato home. During his more than 40
years on the Homes Board, over 4000 applicants have received aid and
assistance from your board, guided by his wise counsel and advice. How
gloriously our brother truly lives in the lives of others!
Possessed of a consuming concern for the welfare of others, he
symbolizes for us the ultimate in brotherly love.

"The great use of life," said the philosopher James, "is to spend it
for something that outlasts it." How marvelous is our brother's investment in life and in the lives of all around him and near him.
As a tribute to their brother trustee, the trustees of Masonic Homes
of California have adopted the following resolution :
RESOLUTION

Whereas, Past Grand Master Charles Albert Adams has been a
devoted trustee of our Masonic Homes for over 40 years; and
Whereas, Brother Adams has during said time rendered extraordinary and unlimited services, and has permanently endeared himself to
our aged and our children, and
Whereas, we his fellow trustees, wish him to know how much we
value his consecrated services in the application of Masonic love and
asistance; now therefore be it
Resolved, That we as trustees of the Masonic Homes, and on behalf
of the entire fraternity, extend to Brother Adams the sincere appreciation of his brethren for making our Masonic Homes a living symbol of
brotherly love and affection.
