The Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple Corporation present their Fourth Annual Report for the fiscal year ended June
30, 1958.
The Board of Trustees met following the close of the 1957 Annual
Communication of Grand Lodge, as is required by the By-Laws, for the
purpose of organization. The election of Brother Phil N. Myers, Deputy Grand Master, Brother Joe L. Shell, Senior Grand Warden, and
Brother Alfred F. Breslauer. Junior Grand Warden, was formally reported to the Board, and on motion duly made, seconded and carried.
they were elected members of the Board.
IN RETROSPECT

In rendering this report on behalf of the Temple Corporation, it is
fitting to give a brief review of its activities since the inception of the
idea of a California Masonic Memorial Temple.
The first impetus to the idea was given by P.G.M. John R. Moore in
his message as Grand Master in 1947. See 1947 Proceedings-page 35:
page 253, Committee on Policy and General Purposes; page 267, Committee on Finance.
True, the record is indelibly clear that the need was felt prior to
1947, for a review shows that numerous resolutions had been presented
to Grand Lodge in prior years for such purposes as assigning seats for
delegates, limiting the number of Past Masters and other such ideas.
In 1947, Grand Master Moore said in part, "In addition to serving
as a memorial to our brothers who served and died in World War II. a
new temple would furnish a comfortable meeting place for the delegates
to our Communications in the years to come and would provide a fitting
place in which to pause and acknowledge our debt to the early builders
of Masonry in California whose consummate wisdom, fidelity and courage have placed in our hands this magnificent heritage."
It was the hope of the then Grand Master that the proposed new
temple should be ready for occupancy in time for our Centennial Communication in 1950. The record of course is clear that while this Grand
Lodge in its conservatism was not willing to move that fast, we did make
some progress each year. It was not possible under the circumstances to
carry out all of the recommendations of the then Grand Master. but the
idea of a Memorial Building in memory of our war dead brethren has
been carried out, not only in overall design, but also through sculpture
on the California Street side, and by inscription in the memorial foyer.
Thus the new Temple "does in fact provide a fitting place in which to
pause and acknowledge our debt to the early builders of Masonry in

Part of the detail above recorded for prior years is reviewed in part

THE TEMPLE Is BUILT

Bids were opened on March 13, 1956. The "Notice of Completion"
was filed on April 24, 1958. Final payment to the contractor was made
on July 15, 1958. During the span of two years and forty-three days a
dream of the Masons of California became a reality.
At this Annual Communication, in the presence of the regularly
elected delegates to this Grand Lodge and our guests from around the
world our California Masonic Memorial Temple in all its splendor is
presented for inspection and dedication. In presenting this new Temple
to this gathering we do it with confidence. Our experience in its use since
completion has been most gratifying. The comments by those attending
concerts, lectures, or other meetings have been most generous in their
praise as to its beauty, accoustics, comfort and utility. The thousands of
brethren and friends who have taken one of the "Sunday guided tours"
have been equally generous in their praise. The Masons of California,
and all who made it possible, can take pride in their having become a
"Temple Builder."

Earthquake Insurance:
The matter of earthquak e insurance on the California Masonic Memorial Temple has received long and serious study by your Building
Committee. the lending banks, the California Rating Bureau. our Insurance Advisor and the Insurance Committee of Grand Lodge.
In order that the printed record of Grand Lodge on this matter be

May 17, 1956
Mr. Merritt Rowland
Thompkins & Co.
111 Sutter Street
San Francisco, California
Re: California Masonic Memorial Temple
San Francisco, California
Dear Mr. Rowland:
We have reviewed the plans for the captioned structure and have
analyzed these plans from the standpoint of the earthquake hazard. A
field inspection of the site has also been made.
The building is being built on a steep slope on Nob Hill. Foundation
conditions are good. Soil investigations reveal that the structure is
found in a location containing sandstones or other relatively good bearing materials.
The importance of this good foundation material is not to be underestimated. A careful and detailed study made by the California Earthquake Commission after the San Francisco 1906 Earthquake reveals
that, while the earthquake was "Very violent (Grade A) " in the waterfront areas a short distance away, it was only "Strong (Grade D)" in
the vicinity of the Temple.
We would not consider the fact that the Temple is on a steep hillside
to be of any particular concern in this instance. ·
The building will be somewhat "L" shaped. Lower floors, walls, columns, etc., are entirely of reinforced concrete construction. The upper
floors are steel frame, fireproofed with concrete. Relatively few openings
exist in the exterior walls due to the type of occupancy. Occupancy requirements also dictate relatively few partitions.
The materials chosen are well suited for resisting heavy earthquake
forces as compared with some of the lighter, but much weaker, materials
finding some vogue today. Earthquake bracing is provided by the concrete roof and floors, acting as diaphragms (horizontal beams) and the
exterior walls acting as shear walls (bracing walls). The relatively few
wall openings have added materially to the earthquake strength of the
exterior walls.
No known earthquake fault is known to exist in the vicinity. The
San Andreas Fault, on which occurred the 1906 Earthquake, is about 10
miles to the west. As long as a structure is not located directly within a
fault zone, it is more important ~o have good design and good construe-

161

tion rather than place the structure on a site only several miles further
away from a fault.
Predicting earthquakes as to exact time, place, and severity is impossible with our present state of knowledge. However, we do know that
earth strains are building up. The Farrallon Islands are moving northward at the rate of about 2" per year with respect to Oakland. When the
strains become too large, another large earthquake can be expected.
In the event of a repetition of the San Francisco 1906 Shock, it is
probable that the Temple will suffer, at the most, up to 5% damage;
Should a less severe earthquake occur, as a Long Beach ( 1933) Earthquake or an Arvin-Tehachapi-Bakersfield ( 1952) Earthquake, damage
will undoubtedly be less.
The foregoing estimates are based on the building being constructed
in strict conformance with the plans. We understand that a full-time inspector is on the job, and that laboratory tests are being made to insure
that the materials will be up to specification.
Very truly yours,
Very truly yours,
KARL

v. STEINBRUGGE

This letter will amplify our letter of April 3rd. At the time of our
previous inspection, much of the green concrete which had been subjected to the March 22, 1957, earthquake was still covered by its forms.
Accompanied by Mr. Herbert Lyell of H. J. Brunnier's office, we reinspected the structure on May 3, 1957. Special attention was given to
the areas having concrete poured March 18th and March 22nd:
March 18-Two holes about 3'0'' square in west wall where bracing went through 6" curbs on B and D decks at duct
openings.

at duct openings.

wall from col. E-90 through H-90 and H-63 to L-63
from elevation 82'0'' to 91 '8" was poured.

the green concrete as a result of the earthquake of March 22, 1957.

163

We also include the following quotations taken from the special report published by the Rating Bureau in 1956: "The building is designed
to resist strong lateral forces. The probable damage to this structure in
a strong prolonged shock, similar to that of 1906, would be minimum."
Taken from the report of the professional engineer who was retained by Thompkins & Company-Ge neral Insurance Brokers: "In the
event of a repetition of the San Francisco 1906 shock, it is probable
that the Temple will suffer, at the most, up to 5% damage."
In a letter addressed to the Board of Trustees of the Temple Corporation dated May 31, 1956, from Thompkins & Company, Insurance
Broker, this conclusion is reached\ "The conclusion of professional
opinions is that the Temple Building will be probably one of the most
earthquake resistive buildings on the Pacific Coast. The rates reflect it,
and the stated opinions give the conclusion additional support."
It may be noted in passing that during the time of the earthquake the
structural steel was in place and the Vermont Marble Company was
placing marble near the roof top on the Taylor Street side. There was
no damage to this installation.
During construction we did carry primary earthquake coverage.
After completion the lending banks elected not to require earthquake
insurance.
Based on the aforesaid the Board of Trustees have elected not to
carry earthquake coverage on the California Masonic Memorial Temple.
This policy is consistent with the practice followed by the owners of all
of the buildings we checked in San Francisco and which have been constructed during the recent past.

After Payment of Debt, Article-Third (a) of the Articles of Incorporation, would come into play:
Third: "That the specific and primary purposes for which this Corporation is formed are as follows:
(a) "To hold title to certain real property upon which a building to
be known as the California Masonic Memorial Temple is to be erected, to
collect income therefrom, and to turn over the entire amount thereof, less
expenses, to the Endowment Fund of the Masonic Homes of California,
a non-profit corporation organized exclusively for charitable purposes
and to provide office space free of charge for said Masonic Homes of
California."
The California Masonic Memorial Temple Corporation was organized to operate exclusively for charitable purposes and pursuant to the
General Non-Profit Corporation Law of the State of California.
To be debt free will accomplish these important objectives:
1. Reduce the per capita tax for all lodges;
2. To make additional funds available for the Endowment Fund of
the Masonic Homes of California;
3. To bring to complete realization the pride of ownership one feels
owning his own home debt free.

MERIT RoLL PLAQUE

As of June 30, 1958, there were 340 lodges out of 685 participating
lodges in California and Hawaii which have achieved the Merit Roll by
contributing an average of at least $10.00 per member to the Memorial
Temple Building Fund. Since then twelve additional lodges have reached
Merit Roll status.
In working o"ut the detail your Board of Trustees decided that since
Grand Lodge voted that lodges could have their names recorded on the
plaque at any time until the debt on the Temple is paid in full, that we
would have a plaque designed to provide for such additions. The permanent Memorial Plaque is in place on the second floor opposite the elevators. There is a space provided for the name of each lodge. Those
lodges with "Merit Roll" status will find their name and number recorded. Your Board of Trustees has such implicit faith in all the lodges
of California and Hawaii that we felt providing space for less than
all and for a reasonable number of new lodges to be formed could
be a major error in judgment. The plaque is now in place to be viewed
with pride by all visitors to the Temple.

PRESS PREVIEW
Invitations and press kits were sent to daily and weekly papers
throughout California and Hawaii. Included also in this group were
radio and television stations. About 60 press, radio and T.V. representatives devoted about 4Yi hours of their day to the Temple. Coverage
was national. Press representatives came from as far as Los Angeles.
BANKERS' PREVIEW
We had as our guests 15 top bankers representing the banks who
assisted in the financing of the Temple. We wanted them to see their
collateral. They must have been impressed for after the tour, and while
at luncheon, we were smothered delightfully with praise and commendation. This we gladly accepted on behalf of all "Temple Builders."

The California Masonic Memorial Temple has been under contemplation since 1947, when its construction was first recommended to the
Grand Lodge. The voluntary fund-raising campaign within the membership of our Lodges was started in 1954. Since then 120,731 individual
contributions, totaling $1,858,358, have been made by the Masons of
California and Hawaii, their families, and friends. Of the 683 Lodges in
California and Hawaii, 332 have achieved the Merit Roll, by contributing an average of at least 10 per member to the Memorial Temple Building Fund. T ,h e Open Book recording the accomplishment of these
Lodges will remain open for the inclusion of additional Lodges until
December 31, 1958. (Since extended to March 31, 1959. )

The special program preceding the symphony consisted of a word of
welcome by the Grand Master, invocation by the Grand Chaplain, the
contractor turning the keys over to the architect, the architect presenting
them to the Grand Master, and the Grand Master turning them over to
the President of the Temple Corporation.
Just for the record. The key used in the ceremony is a gold plated key
presented through the courtesy of the Schlage Lock Comany.
The ushering for the two symphony programs was done by De
Malay boys from the Bay Area chapters. They did themselves proud.
From press clippings and expressions of the 3,200 Masons and
friends present the opening night was an outstanding success and wi11
long be remembered.

¥:i~-~~:.. :::=::::::::::::::::::::::=::::::::::=::~~~

The California Masonic Memorial Temple is open every business
day, Monday through Friday, 8:45 A.M. to 4:45 P.M.
Sundays: 2:00 ~ 5:00 P.M. for guided tours, temporarily only.
Saturdays reserved for special groups by appointment.
Beginning with the first Sunday in June. and each Sunday since,
except a few Sundays when the building has been occupied, we have
shown an average of about 700 brethren, their families and friends
through the building. It is our sincere hope that every brother will be
able to accommodate his time to see the Temple with this schedule. It
belongs to the Masons of California, for a11 to see. The facilities are
for you, use them.
We are ind~d grateful to the 60 brethren of Bay Area lodges who
have given of their time on Sundays to act as guides, showing their
brethren and families and friends through the Temple. Without them it
couldn't have been done.

VISITING HOURS

NEW BROCHURE

Through the courtesy of the Tidewater Oil Company. lessees of the
garage. a new brochure in sufficient quantity for mailing to all Masons
of California lodges has been made available to us.
Your Board of Trustees, on behalf of all of us. here publicly express
our appreciation for their enthusiasm, confidence and cooperation.
LIBRARY AND MusEUM

During the preliminary planning days of the T em.pie. and particu~
larly at the time of our Centennial celebration, there was considerable
talk about a museum in which to house certain of those historic items of
particular interest to Masons. It has been often stated that if such a
place were provided and proper care for security assured, that brethren

177

PROCEEDIN GS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

would make such items of historic interest available for public display.
Your Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Memorial Temple
has provided some space on the second Boor of the foyer where such a
museum could be located. We feel that the initiative for such an undertaking should be left to Grand Lodge.
We also feel that a Masonic library, if provided at all, should be a
function of the Grand Lodge. Space for a modest library room on the
second floor of the foyer has been provided. Additiona l storage space for
book shelving can be made available on the ground floor. The library
and museum, both in the same general area, together with the Merit Roll

PAST GRAND MASTERS PORTRAITS

For many years the Grand Lodge has provided sufficient funds to
have the portrait of the Grand Master painted.
In the old building at 25 Van Ness Avenue. the portraits of the living
Past Grand Masters were hung in the foyer of the Grand Lodge office.
On the death of a Past Grand Master the portrait started the last mile
down the hall; the end one always going into basement storage to make
room for the portrait of the most recent candidate .
The question of continuing this practice has been debated long and
loud. There is an honest difference of opinion. A policy decision should
be made by Grand Lodge.
It is therefore suggested that:
( 1 ) Painting of portraits of the incoming Grand Master and subsequent Grand Masters be deferred;
( 2) That the Grand Master be requested to appoint a suitable committee to study this whole problem of portraits, and present its findings
and recommendations to the next session of this Grand Lodge.
· Their study should include the matter of continuing the painting of
portraits and, if continued, the disposition to be made of them. And
also what disposition should be made of the present portraits now in
storage. if any alternate plan, such as photograp hs is recommended.

REPORT OF THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS COMMITTE E

How ready to cooperate are the students, parents. and school personnel when a lodge committee carefully plans, organizes, and offers
the program-not for the publicity of the lodge or the school and school
people, but for the benefit of the pupil-the girl and the boy concerned.
Awards are the foundation for motivating fine public school good
work.
The fourth-Gradu ation time is a time when Masonic Lodges
extend very valuable evidence of loyalty to public education. At this
time scholarships or grants of aid to graduates who are going on and
need assistance are offered. Public school administrators will tell what
honors, recognitions, and scholarship awards will enrich the graduation exercises and stimulate young people to strive for better attainment.
The fifth-During the annual observance of Public Schools Week
in the spring season so very much is already known that but momentary reference is made to this event which is one of the country's
greatest school and community experiences the fraternity stimulates.
No other Masonic leadership event in the field of completely unselfish service to our greatest heritage--the public school-is known
in other states in our Union which compares with California's Annual
Public Schools Week. The thoughts of more than one and a half
million souls turn to thoughts of public education with no thought of
racial. creedal, political, or socio-economic status as a fundmental to
the needs to know what is the very best for our public schools.

MAKING OPERATIVE OUR l.oYALTY AS MASONS TO PUBLIC EDUCATION

Every Blue Lodge Mason who has been to lodge, read his lodge
bulletin or who has. talked about Masonry in California knows that
Masons are at work. The vivid realization that Masonry is at its best
when it is operative has caused every phase of Masonic organization
to search out individual. group, state-wide aspects of American life
into whkh can be penetrated an advantageous expression of interest,
support. and advancement.
A most natural, normal. and appealing area of expression for operative Masonry is the 6.eld of public education. These then become the
current facets of Masonic expression which are the reasons why, during Public Schools Week 1958, the following have been realized:

an awareness of Public Schools Week purposes and reasons for observance.
2. There were held some 8500 events, occasions, visitation programs, assemblies, speaking appearances, demonstrations, and community -gatherings-al l dedicated to belief in public education, loyalty
to teachers, faith in youth, and a determination to help public schools
be at their · best.
3. To these various observances an estimated two million persons
gave presence. attention, and interest.

WHAT THE PEOPLE OP CALIFORN IA WANT IN THEIR PUBLIC SCHOOLS

Study of the results of the broad state-wide interest stimulated by
the Fraternity of Freemaso nry in public education and public schools
revealed many valuable thoughts.
This year 1t was especially desired to learn what the public wants
in their public schools. The following are direct expression s and are
outcomes of public school lodge committee work:
People wantFirst-par ents want good teachers. When they describe "good
teachers" they say things like well-train ed, kind, friendly, healthy,
attractive and neat, sense of humor, and glad to see parents.
Second-P arents want good solid teaching, learning, and discipline
in their schools.

cation of Brother Oscar Lawler and expressed the regret of all present
that severe illness had prevented Brother Lawler from attending this
Communication. The Grand Master then presented the following:
This is the portrait of a great man, a great lawyer, a great American
and a great Mason. Our Senior Past Grand Master was elected
Grand Master of Masons in California on October 16, 1908, and today
we shall celebrate with him his Golden Annivers ary-SO years of service
to Freemaso nry as a Past Grand Master.
The story of Oscar Lawler is an American story, built and indelibly
welded into the history of Los Angeles, of California and of the United
States. He was born in Marshallt own, Iowa, on April 2, 1875, the
fifth of ten children. The whole family worked and Oscar started in the
fields of the neighboring farms and with the family chores of milking,
gardening and so forth. When about 11 years old, he became the janitor
of the local public school. sweeping, setting the fires in the old stoves,
hauling ashes, shoveling snow and all the rest of that job at $10 per
month.
In 1888 the family moved to Los Angeles, which was experiencing a
"hangove r" from the 1887 boom. Jobs were scarce, but that didn't stop
Oscar Lawler; however, it did stop his schooling. He sold newspape rs,
was a cash-boy in a dry goods store at $2.50 per week, a Western Union
messenger at $20 per month, and hall boy at the California Club at $25
per month. In 1918 he became president of that club.
When about 15 years old, while working at the California Club, he
started to stud}' law on his own. Confused by the legal phrases, he
appealed to Henry O'Melven y for advice and then reorganize d his
studies.
Shortly thereafter he quit the club, janitored to pay his tuition and
learned shorthand and typewritin g. With this learned, he entered the
employ of Leo Longley, an official court reporter. The work was hard,
requiring long and late hours of transcribin g court testimony and
Longley arranged for Oscar to do stenograp hic work for Judge Erskine
M. Ross and the United States Attorney so that he could continue his
study of law. During these times, our distinguis hed brother met and
establishe d lasting friendships with many of the great leaders of that
period.
After a long struggle to earn his own living and at the same time
study law, Oscar was admitted to practice law in 1896 and his struggles
as a lawyer commenced. He paid his office rent by doing stenograp hic
work for his associates, gathered momentum as a lawyer, formed a
partnershi p and was on his way to fame.
Becoming interested in civic affairs, Oscar became a precinct worker
for his party, then chairman of its City Conventio n, its County Con-

187

PROCEEDINGS OP THE

GRAND LODGE OP CALIFORNIA

vention, and in 1904 a delegate to the National Convention which nominated that great and active Mason, Theodore Roosevelt, for President.

for and service to his city, his state, his nation and his fellowman, it is
only natural that his Masonic career should be equally distinguished .
Raised in East Gate (then Sunset) Lodge No. 290 on April 22, 1898,
Oscar became its ·Master in 1901. Oscar and other distinguished
brethren formed a temple association and the lodge building was
constructed and paid for. Service as secretary of the Los Angeles
Masonic Board of Relief was added to his record. With the disastrous
earthquake and fire in San Francisco in 1906, Oscar and Motley Flint,
the then Grand Master, spent weeks in this city bringing relief to the
distressed, the homeless and the suffering. Again, the story of those
times and what was done under great difficulties would constitute a book
in itself. Suffice it to say, another chapter in the service of this great
Mason to his brethren and his state!
While serving his government, a visit to Washington D.C., which
included a trip to George Washington's Lodge, brought to Oscar's
attention the fire and other hazards which might obliterate the priceless
relics relating to this great American and Mason. This distinguished
brother of ours suggested a nationwide project to erect an appropriate
fireproof building in which they could be housed and after many conferences Worshipful Brother Charles Callahan, then Master of Alexandria-Washington Lodge No. 22, called the original meeting from
which sprang the George Washington Masonic Memorial on Shooters
Hill in Virginia.
Oscar Lawler was elected Junior Grand Warden in 1906 and with
the untimely death of Deputy Grand Master Reuben H. Lloyd was
elected Grand Master in 1908. Again he served with distinction, traveling about the statE; by train and horse and carriage to visit with his
brethren and carry on the duties of his office. Through his efforts a
home was founded for the children of our distressed and deceased
brethren at San Gabriel, and the foundation laid for our present home
at Covina, a landmark in our history.
Since Oscar Lawler came to California in 1888 our country has
passed through three wars and changed from a farming to an industrial giant. Los Angeles, from a sleepy Mexican town, has advanced to
a foremost place among world cities, and California, from a remote and
distant national stepchild, has become a great agricultural, industrial,
financial and maritime center of constantly increasing stature.
The bicycle has come, flourished, and, with the horse, receded to
minor importance as a means of transportation: the telephone has outrun
the telegraph. and both are overshadowed by radio and television.
Trucks and buses, long encroaching on railroads and steamships, are
being superseded by the airplane; oil has replaced coal, diesel is rapidly
displacing steam, and electricity, impinging both, is itself threatened by
atomic power. Shorthand reporting has been mechanically supplanted,
and tape-recording and television are realities. Crowned heads have
become largely a memory, the British Empire has given up its colonial

. I~ 1905 our ~rother became United States Attorney for the Southern
District of California and handled many of the cases which made
history and changed the course of events. I wish I had the time to review

served _with such distinction that in 1909 President Taft appointed him
an Assistant Attorney General of the United States and he was assigned
t~ the Department of the Interior. In this capacity he again displayed
his greatness and ability in the handling of cases and activities which
made history. For example, at the time the Colorado River broke from

was sent by President Taft to secure the consent of President Diaz of

this catastrophe and correct the current situation. It took a lot of work
and ~lanning to get past the anti-American Secretary of the Treasury of
Mexico and reach President Diaz, but this was done and the necessary
approval was secured.
Who in California has not heard of the bombing of the Los Angeles
Times in 19107 This was not only a catastrophe but the successful
prosecution of the perpetrators of the crime and the exposure of the
mu~derous ring of dynamiters who had spread terror throughout the
?atlo? was a great serv~ce to hu~anity .. Oscar was a most important cog
m th1s great undertaking. Agam I wish I had the time to cover the
multitude of important assignments carried out by our distinguished
brother.
Ironically, it was another bomb which almost ended Oscar's life. On
the night of August 3, 1919, a disgruntled associate of a litigant who had
been defeated through the efforts of Oscar as the opposing attorney
destroyed our brother's home with a home-made bomb. Mr. and Mrs.
~wler ~e~e badly injured, hospitalized for some time, but escaped
with their hves. The Great Architect of the Universe must have been
watching over them that night.
. In his profession and civic activities, Oscar gave unsparingly of his
t~me ~nd talents. He became president of the Los Angeles Bar Association m 1923, served with distinction, and thereafter continued to serve
in the affairs of the county and state bar associations.
Of interest to all of us was Oscar's friendship with another distinguished Mason, Will Rogers, whose tragic death at Point Barrow,
Alaska, brought sorrow to millions. Oscar participated in the arrangements to establish communications with Point Barrow, the arrangements
for the return of the earthly remains, the funeral and the establishment
of memo~ials in. Ne_w York, Oklahoma and Los Angeles ... a friend,
who cherishes his friends and their memories.
With a private and public career such as this, filled with concern

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Investment Committee concludes its eighth year of activity. and
herewith renders its report for the twelve months ending June 30. 1958.
Each year's report gives a certain amount of historical background and
basic information. which should be helpful to those attending Grand
Lodge for the first time.
The Prudent Man Rule in modified form was adopted by Grand
Lodge at its 1950 Communication. For the Constituent Lodges a Prudent Man Rule was adopted in 1951.
The Investment Committee of Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California
was formed for the purpose of administering the investable funds of
Grand Lodge. the Masonic Homes of California and the Masonic
Homes Endowment Fund. The Committee does not supervise the investments of Constituent Lodges. Grand Lodge makes the services of its
investment advisor available to the Lodges. Many Lodges are now making use of this service, as evidenced by the fact that 21i Lodges with
$4.575,000 of investments are now consulting with our investment advisor.
The Investment Committee is composed of the Grand Treasurer, the
Assistant Grand Treasurer. the Chairman of the Finance Committee. the
President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees or a Trustee of that
Board designated by him, and the Chairman of the Masonic Homes Endowment Board or a member of that Board designated by him. The
President of the Masonic Homes Board of Trustees has designated
Brother Past Master Ralph H. Head and the Chairman of the Endowment Board has designated Brother Past Master John W. Davey. as
members of the Committee.
By Ordinance. under Section 246 (formerly 86) with respect to investment of Grand Lodge funds. and Section 403 (formerly 152.1 ) respecting investments by Constituent Lodges, the following provisions
and subsequent amendments were promulgated:
GROUP I. At least 40% of the funds available for investment must
be in:
A)

Cash and/or bank accounts.

B)

Obligations of the United States.

C)

Obligations of the State of California and its political subdivisions.

D)

Such other securities as are legal investments for California
savings banks.

191

GROUP II. Up to 20% may be invested in :
A) Other evidences of indebtedness. which are or will be fully
listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission as a National Securities
Exchan,ge. except that this listing requirement shall not include railroad equipment trust issues ( 1955 ) .
B) Preferred stocks, which are or will be fully listed and registered on an exchange registered with the Securities and
Exchange Commission as a National Securities Exchange.
except that full listing and registration of preferred stock
shall not be required whenever the common stock of the
corporation issuing such preferred stock is fully listed and
registered on such an exchange, provided that such preferred stock is traded on such an exchange ( 1956).
GROUP III. Up to 40% may be invested in :
A) Common stocks. which must be fully listed and registered
on an exchange registered with the Securities and Exchange
Commission as a National Securities Exchange, except that
this listing requirement shall not apply to bank and insurance stocks.
B) Shares of Investment Trusts.
C) Shares and/or certificates of insured Federal Savings or
Building and Loan Associations ( 1957). The amount invested in any one association shall not exceed the amount
covered by insurance. (THIS AMENDMENT APPLIES

ONLY TO CONSTITUENT LODGES AND DOES
NOT.APPLY TO THE INVESTMENT OF GRAND
LODGE FUNDS).
With respect to the authority to invest in Groups II and III. the
Ordinances read as follows: "No such investments. however. shall be
made which at the time of purchase will result in the total market value
of the securities referred to in this section exceeding twenty per cent (or
forty per cent) of the total market value of all the cash, bank accounts
and securities held,"-the controlling point being that there cannot be
more than 20% or 40% invested in Groups II and III. respectively, at

the time of purchase.
Since its formation the Investment Committee has met regularly
every three months. Between quarterly meetings the business of the
Committee is handled by correspondence or telephone.
As stated, we have just completed eight years of operation. The following is a summary of the consolidated market values of securities
owned. plus investable cash, together with a record of dollar income on
these investments, beginning with November 30, 1950, and for each
succeeding fiscal year, through June 30, 1958, including the percentage
income on the market value of each year.

The book value as of June 30, 1958, was approximately $12,514,675,
and the market value as explained in the consolidated summary was
$12,529,625, or an increase above book value of $14,950. Net profits of
approximately $956,000 were taken prior to June 30, 1958, therefore,
profits taken and appreciation of $14,950 amounted to $970,950. Profits
taken always remain a part of principal.
Contributions, gifts and bequests have also increased the dollar total.
For the twelve months ended June 30, 1958, they totaled approximately
$757,500, including Endowment Fund contributions made through the
Lodges.
The above facts and figures are reported as a matter of information.
In passing, may we also mention that while the total portfolio has
increased since November, 1950, from $6,124,471 to $12,529,625, or
104.58%, at the same time the income based on present holdings, divi~
dends and interest rates, has increased from $120,598 to $496,948, or
312.07%.

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF CONTROL
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Board of Control submits herewith its annual report covering the activities of our eighteen Boards of Relief and six employment bureaus maintained within the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge
of California.
The much publicized recession throughout our country has caused
considerable additional activity in our Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus. In spite of this additional work that has been thrust
upon our executive secretaries and employment managers, your Board
finds that all offices are discharging their duties promptly and efficiently. We wish to commend these devoted Masons and also let them
know that their e1forts are greatly appreciated by Masons not only in
our grand jurisdiction but also all the ·grand jurisdictions in the United
States and throughout the world. As a further indication of their devotion, we would also like to point out that some of these executive secretaries in the smaller boards work without financial remuneration.
The many and varied activities of our Boards of Relief and Employment Bureaus have often been brought to your attention in these annual reports. We will, therefore, not go into detail in this report as
to all these activities. In our eighteen boards, "relief" of one kind
or another to worthy Brother Master Masons and those dependent
upon them constitutes by far the most important and time consuming
portion of the work. This relief is granted in many ways ranging from
direct financial assistance to finding steady employment for those who
call at our offices.
There is one type of relief seldom mentioned but is greatly appreciated by the recipients. This relief has to do with the furnishing of
hospital beds, wheel chairs, walkers. traction equipment, and rails. In
this connection, we recently received a communication from our Long
Beach Board of Relief wherein they advised us that they own, by
purchase or gift, four complete hospital beds, four metal wheel chairs,
three walkers, and other miscellaneous items, such as traction equipment and rails. All of these items are available free of charge to any
master Mason or member of his immediate family. The saving to
those using these items runs into many thousands of dollars per year.
The Board of Control heartily approves this type of relief and recommends that boards who are not now in a position to furnish such relief
investigate the possibility of procuring this type of equipment.
BOARDS OF RELIEF

We have in our grand jurisdiction eighteen Boards of Relief. All
of these boards are furnished copies of a Standard Practice Bulletin
prepared by a nationally known accounting firm under the direction
of the Board of Control and with the approval of the Grand Master.

197

This Standard Practice Bulletin outlines in detail a uniform method
for not only keeping all the financial accounts in order but also the
statistical information required by the Board of Control. By making
use of this uniform system of keeping accounts and records, the Board
of Control is able to make comparisons of the various offices and also
readily provide to the Finance Committee and Grand Lodge the financial and statistical data required.
The reports from our eighteen Boards of Relief for the Masonic
year ending June 30, 1958 have been carefully studied by your Board
of Control. and we submit the following for your information:

EMPLOYMENT BUREAUS

Boards of Relief may, with the consent of the Board of Control
form Employment Bureaus. In our grand jurisdiction, we presently
have six of these Employment Bureaus. The following figures give an
idea of the extent of this activity:
Registered for Employment. ......................................... 7,027
Jobs secured ·····················---·-······································· 1,515
Positions offered by employers .................................... 4,167
There is no charge of any kind made to either the employee or the
employer for this type of service. As you know, the private "fee"
employment agencies make a charge to either the employee or the
employer for all placements. The amount of fee permissible to charge
is regulated by the State of California. Using this same fee schedule
as a basis, we have calculated that the number of Masons and their
families who secured jobs through our employment bureaus saved the
sum of $122,167.37.

our Masonic brethren, their widows, and members of their immediate
families is a worthwhile type of relief. However, we are greatly concerned about the steadily rising cost of maintaining our six Employment Bureaus and will continue to find ways and means to reduce these
costs.

REIMBURSEMENTS TO MASONIC BoARDS OP RELIEF

The San Francisco Board of Relief has requested reimbursements
in the amount of $423.68, which covers six different cases. Brother
Andrew Burke, Executive Secretary of the San Francisco Board of
Relief. has been working on these cases for a number of years and has
been unable to obtain reimbursements. One case in particular having
to do with a brother from Okinawa Lodge No. 118, Okinawa, dates
back to the year 1953. Another case having to do with a brother belonging to a lodge in Scotland goes back close to five years. We
mention this merely to indicate that our executive secretaries work
long and diligently on these cases before asking for reimbursements.
It is the opinion of the Board of Control that the San Francisco
Board of Relief should be reimbursed in each of these six cases. We
have presented the full details of these cases to the Finance Committee together with our recommendation for approval.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CHARTERS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons
of the State of California:
MANUAL FOR THE FORMATION OF A MASONIC LODGE

At present there is no complete manual or other collected or compiled
reference work to inform and guide those brethren seeking to form
new lodges. The necessary information must be sought out at various
sections in the Masonic Code, by inquiry of the Grand Secretary, and by
inquiry of Inspectors or other brethren who have had some experience
on the subject.
Your committee seeks to alleviate this situation. Through the primary
efforts of a sub-committee composed of Kenneth L. Hemphill, Robert A.
Smith and Phillip B. Stone, and aided by suggestions and constructive
criticism by the Assistant Grand Secretary, Henry D. Oliphant, and the
other members of the Charters Committee, we are ready to present a
final draft of a proposed manual to the Grand Master and Grand Secretary. It is hoped that approval may be obtained, for the publication of
this manual and its distribution to those concerned with the formation
of new lodges, as the occasions arise. We do not request any action on
this by Grand Lodge, as we believe none is required. The subject is
contained in our report merely for your information.

REPORT OF
THE COMMITTEE ON MASONIC HISTORY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The 1957 History Committee report, as submitted to this Grand
Lodge, contained a number of recommendations which form the basis
of this Report.
The development of two history lectures, with colored slides, centered around a number of interesting old Lodges and Temples in California, is well along towards completion. The inclemency of the weather
in early spring. as well as other unforeseen conditions, prevented our
volunteer photographers from getting an early start. However, the pictures are nearly all taken and finishing touches are being put on the
lectures, and we are happy to announce that we are ready to present
them to such lodges as may wish to receive them. A lecture has been
prepared for the North and another for the South. Requests must be
in writing and dates will be assigned in the same order as requests are
received. Please do NOT specify the date, but indicate the day of the
week you would like to have the presentation made and the committee
will assign the first open date on that specific day. We will try to respect
your wishes and will accept as many engagements as our committee
members are able to fill.
Your committee has done little towards the preparation of a onevolume supplemental edition of "One Hundred Years of Freemasonry
in California," but we can report progress in the collection of material
for such a book and will endeavor to place a recommendation before
you at the next Annual Communication. A number of the 4-volume
sets of our Centennial publication are still available, at $25.00 per set.
Again we strongly recommend that every lodge in California should
have a set of this timely and important work on California Masonry.
Again this past year. members of the committee have participated
in a number of regional seminars sponsored by the Research Committee and the research lodges. We were happy to help and hope our contributions were worthwhile.
Despite our calling your attention in our last ,Report to the deplorable condition of Masonic cemetery plots and the graves of departed
Masons, we regret exceedingly that little if any progress has been made
in the removal of rubbish, debris, and weeds under which many of our
brethren lie buried. In our opinion it is to our shame, and an abomination to California Masonry in general and to specific lodges in particular,
that this condition should continue to persist.

FURTHE R, that all applications for official, registered designatio n

All applications shall be governed by the following terms and conditions:
1. Any constituen t lodge in California , having a valid claim to
visible, tangible historic association may apply for designatio n as a
Registered Historic Masonic Landmark , which said designatio n will
be awarded upon a proper showing being made that would justly entitle
the said landmark described in the application to such designation.
(a) .Standards of value from an historical standpoin t, by competen t
persons versed in historical matters will be used as the basis for judging
applications.
2. All applications shall be in writing, on a form furnished for the
purpose by the Grand Lodge Masonic History Committee.
3. Applications shall be submitted and/or considered only when
made by authority of a constituen t lodge under a resolution lawfully
had and attested by the Master and Secretary over the seal of the lodge
affixed thereto.

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL COMMITTE E
ON DE MOLAY
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
"If our country is ever destroyed it will not be because of someone
else's bombs, but because of our own indifference." This wisdom was
given to us by the Grand Orator in his oration before this body last
year. How significant this thought becomes when we observe the
expanding teen-age population of our State, seeking the key to the
future, but having so much difficulty finding it because of the indifference of its elders. The challenge is real. Are we willing to accept it,
or are we going to surrender the minds of these young people to the
influence of philosophies contrary to those which made our country
great.
The Order of De Molay, with its emphasis on the principles which
are so dear to Masonry. holds out the key to the future to those who
come under its influence. The lessons of filial love, religion, courtesy.
comradeship, fidelity, cleanness and patriotism taught in De Molay
Chapters under the leadership of the members of our Craft can have a
profound effect on their future.
The effects of this Grand Lodge's policy permitting constituent
lodges to sponsor chapters of the Order of De Molay, thus maintaining the necessary adult leadership on the highest plane possible,
have been most noticeable during the past year. Fifty-one constituent lodges are presently sponsoring De Molay Chapters in this State.
One third of these are new chapters in communities that rely on the
Blue Lodge for all of its Masonic influence. A new enthusiasm and
awareness of purpose has been developed through the interest of local
lodges in the affairs of the Order of De Molay.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
Your committee continues to receive and review the proceedings
of most of the grand jurisdictions of the world. Short summaries of
many of these reviews are published in the California Freemason.
Section 203 of our Ordinances provides that in addition to its usual
and customary duties the committee on Correspondence shall publish
and distribute the magazine "California Freemason." This task now
constitutes the major part of the work of the committee.
We have now completed the fifth year of publication of this quarterly which has filled the need for an official Grand Lodge publication.
Each year the editorial policy and the selection of articles is under the
direct control of the then Grand Master. Since 1955 a style policy has
been approved which in part is as follows:
"Strive for short sentences and short paragraphs.
"Use a factual style and avoid meaningless adjectives.
"Avoid 'small town' newspaper style which bristles with compliments.
"Follow modern usage and use capital letters sparingly. Exceptions
in our field: Mason, Masonic, Freemason, Craft. Capitalize lodge only
when referring to a particular lodge, likewise with the words master,
mason, grand lodge, worshipful master, etc.
"Designate a lodge as Johnstown Lodge No. 999.
"As far as possible avoid 'most worshipful,' 'very worshipful' and
other forms of address-natural in the lodge room hut pompous in print.
Try 'Grand Master John Jones,' 'Masonic Inspector William ·Brown,'
etc.
"Prefer 'Freemason' over "Mason,' 'Freemasonry' over 'Masonry,'
hut usage permits the shorter form.
"Avoid such terms as 'Raised to the sublime degree of master mason.'
Try 'He became a master mason.' The first should he reserved for
private conversation.
"A by-line is given to articles written by elected grand lodge officers
and by past grand masters. Articles by members of the Correspondence
Committee are frequently unsigned, hut like other articles may have the
author's name in six point type at the end.''

REPORT OF COMMITTEE
ON CONSTITUTION OBSERVANCE
Brethren:
Meeting as we are, at the close of the Observance Period, we can
report more fully on this year's celebrations than last when the Communication was held before the close of the event. Even so, we have
very little on which to base our report as only 29.7% of the Lodges
have so far reported. Last year, after all reports were in, a total of only
39.4% of the lodges reported. Both years, Masters were requested
to fill out the report form found on the last page of our published booklet, a copy of which was sent to each Master by the Grand Secretary's
office. We cannot refrain from commenting that the failure of these
Masters in reporting the work of their lodges on an official Grand
Lodge activity is, in our opinion, inconsistent with the duties and
responsibilities of the Master of a lodge and even may be indicative
of violation of their obligations and the Charges which they promised
to fulfill at the time of their induction into the Master's chair: for it
is conceivable that among those lodges not reporting there are some
who held no Constitution Observance program at all and others who
rendered lip service to the words of the Grand Master's Proclama-

213

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

tion but did not at all observe the spirit of it. Much as we dislike injecting a discorda nt note into this particula r Communication, which ought
to be one of joyous rejoicing, this had to be called to your attention
for it is once again indicative of the apathy and disintere stedness too
prevalen t among the craft and which we belabore d at length in our
last Report to this Grand Lodge.
It is the unanimous opinion of the subcommittee of 10 members
out of 15 which drafted this report that the lodges of the jurisdiction
should either give 100% spirited support to any proclamation of the
Grand Master, or to any edict or ordinanc e of this Grand Lodge and
when they feel they cannot do so, or are unwilling, then to avail
themselves of the remedies at hand which is the repeal of the legislation. This committee recommends that the incoming committee for
1959 include as a part of their work a careful examination of the form
and characte r of the Observa nce program as well as of all phases and
aspects appertain ing thereto and that they place before this Grand
Lodge at its next annual Communication their recommendations, if
any, with respect to their findings.
From the Master's reports so far submitte d we feel we should comment on three matters of unusual interest emerging out of the work
of this committee. They are:
1. On the whole, the attendan ce so far reported at Observa nce
celebrations this year is somewh at improved over last year. It appears
this is due in part to a greater reliance on the "Guide" booklet already
referred to in which new ideas are proposed and also to better planning on the part of the lodge committees. Where it is apparent that
lodges started well in advance of the Septemb er celebration period and
put in consider able thought and hard work, their celebrations have on
the whole been successful.
2. Particula r notice should be taken of the Merced celebration
which took place this past week and which we point to as an example
of what we believe the Grand Master and this Grand Lodge wishes
to accomplish. The lodges there joined together . In addition to a
consider able run of newspap er publicity the Merced committee, under
the able direction of Brother George Wolf, altogeth er inspired or was
responsible for eleven separate meetings devoted to celebrating the
birthday of our Constitu tion. These meetings took place before service
clubs, schools, and in the lodge hall. At one public school meeting,
devoted entirely to this subject, 1900 students were in attendan ce. Last
year, the Merced celebration was one of the most outstand ing in the
state. The Merced Lodges are to be commended for the spirit and
vigor with which they have prosecut ed this program and this committee hopes and prays that this same spirit will become contagio us
and spread from district to district. Probably what is most importan t,
is what this spirit is doing to bring Masonry to the notice of the pro-

fane and to promote the craft as a live, virile organiza tion inducing
respect and becoming the envy of all good people everywhere. Certainly this is one of the things we can do to arouse interest which in
tum ought to stimulate applications for membership.
3. The eleven lodges of eastern Contra Costa county joined together for the first time in their celebration and while the magnitud~
of their undertak ing, and the timing. has forced a postponement until
after his Communication, the work so far done is portento us and
may have great significance for the craft in Californ ia for years to
come. A working committee comprised of one brother from each
lodge was formed, with a chairman. This committee became a "Citizen's Advisory Committee," which intereste d the county-w ide Junior
College District in the promotion and staging of an Observa nce ce~e­
bration. The college district is operatin g two separate campuses with
an enrollment of well over 7000 full and part time students . The
administ rative staff and a faculty committee fully discussed the project
and came forward with a proposal that the Junior College District
EACH YEAR HEREA FTER sponsor what is to be known as
"Americ an Heritage Day," alternati ng between the two campuses.
The underlyi ng theme of "Americ an Heritage Day," will be our Constitution which makes possible our America n way of life. Each year,
the immediate subject will center on one phase of America n freedom
under the Constitution. This year, the Constitu tion itself; next, our
free enterpris e system; the next, the labor movement: the Free Public
Schools: Freedom to Worship ; Freedom of the Press; American Scientific Progress , etc. The program s will include student participation but
outside authoriti es .will also be brought in. Wide and thorough newspaper publicity is being released by special staff assistant s, aided by
the Citizen's Advisory Committee in their respective communities.
The committee set up by our lodges has been amplified and enlarged
to include representatives from the Central Labor Council, the Contra
Costa County Bar Association, the County Historica l Society an~
the D. A. R., and before this week is out it is expected the veterans
organiza tions, the Native Sons and Daughte rs, and the three major
service club organiza tions will join. In addition, the two daily newspapers and one weekly. at consider able cost to them, will run full pa~e
printings of the Constitu tion with recognition of the sponsori ng bodies
along the borders of the page. The celebration will be held on a
Sunday afternoo n on the college campus. Several copies of the outline of the program are in the hands of this committee and may be had
upon application so far as they go. Last Monday , this annual project
was presente d to the Board of Trustees of Contra Costa Junior College who unanimously approved it as a community program to occur
each year.
Mention should be made of the efforts of the corps of inspectors
for San Francisco, in promotin g a joint program held in this auditorium

Most Worshipful and Brethren:
You will recall that last year's report of this committee recommended that all Mutual Aid Associations disassociate themselves
entirely from lodge sponsorship, pursuant to Section 333 of the
Masonic Code, and that they obtain the approval of the State Insurance Commissioner. Failure to do so within six months was to result
in dissolution. Certain specific requirements were enumerated as indicia of complete separation from lodge sponsorship. Likewise, certain
methods of dissolution were discussed and approved.
The committee is happy to inform you that none of these associations are now operating contrary to either State or Masonic law. Eleven
of the smaller associations voluntarily dissolved by methods approved
by your committee. The remaining thirty, including all of the larger
ones, are operating with the written approval of the State Insurance
Commissioner, and have fully complied with Section 333 of the Ma..
sonic Code. Furthermore , the compliance or dissolution of these organizations was prompt and, with a few excusable exceptions, was
within the six months period. Documenta ry evidence of compliance
has been flied with the Grand Secretary. The accepted and traditional
concept of Masonic charity is in nowise being violated at the present
time by any of the constituent ·lodges. Furthermore , neither the Grand
Lodge nor the constituent lodges are now subject to the embarrassment of having a group of Masons function contrary to State law.
At the same time, the rights of individual Masons to enter into a
legitimate and worthwhile joint undertaking has been preserved.
In conclusion, the Committee wishes to express its sincere appreciation to the Mutual Aid Association officers and the inspectors who
assisted so materially in clarifying and solving this Grand Lodge problem. We are likewise grateful to our present and immediate past Grand
Masters for this opportunity of service and for their fine cooperation.
As there appears to be no further need for the Special Committee
on Mutual Aid Associations, we recommend that it be discontinued
after the acceptance of this report.
Fraternally yours,
WAKEFIELD TAYLOR
LEVIN
GERALD
KENNETH THOMPSON
F. WESLEY DAVIES
RALPH T. MERRIAM

IN MEMORIAM .

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

MEMOR IAL SERVIC E

IRA DANFORD WHEELER
Ira Danford Wheeler was born June 29, 1884, in Butte County, South
Dakota. He died at the home of his daughter, Mrs. Robert E. Kelleher,
in Los Angeles. His wife predeceas ed him by several years.
Brother Wheeler was raised in Santa Monica Lodge No. 307 on
December 4, 1907. Had he lived a month and a half longer he was to
have received his Fifty-Yea r Button. Much of his time was devoted to
Masonry. He served Santa Monica Lodge No. 307 in various chairs and
stations. In 1925 he was elected Senior Warden of the lodge. At that
time it was felt that a new lodge ought to be formed and Brother Wheeler
was urged to lead in this undertakin g. His efforts were crowned with
success, and in 1926 Palisades Lodge No. 637 was instituted with Ira
Danford Wheeler its first Master. He served this lodge as Secretary from
1927 to 1940, and as Treasurer from 1944 to 1953. To the end he rarely
missed any of its meetings and had a distinguished record of service in the
lodge.
Brother Wheeler was regular in his attendanc e at Grand Lodge, not
having missed an Annual Communication for over thirty years. He
served as Grand Marshal in 1936, and was appointed a member of the
Endowme nt Board in October, 1938. He remained a member of that
important board up to the time of his death, being one of its oldest
members, and serving with zeal and fidelity down through the years.
Brother Wheeler headed his own insurance agency throughou t his
business career. Outside of his business and his lodge. his chief interest
was tennis. His daughter, Gracyn Wheeler Kelleher, who survives him,
was ranked amon~ the first ten in the national list of Women Amateur
Players for several years.
Brother Wheeler was a devoted Mason, his interest never lagged,
and his influence for constructi ve progress was constant. We of this
Grand Lodge are fortunate to have had the services and friendship of
our departed Brother.

. Nevin
Harold Mueller, Organist

REPORT OF THE COMMI TTEE ON NECROL OGY
To the Most Worshipf ul Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
This is a year of rejoicing and victory. The Temple, for which we
have ·l onged and labored over many years, is now complete and has been
dedicated with the solemn formalities of our Craft. We are all happy to
have the high privilege of being present at this, the first Annual Communication of Grand Lodge in its new Temple. There is, however, a large
group of our membership which has not been privileged to be present in
the body. Many of the group worked for this great achievement, but
they did not live to see the fulfillment of their efforts. God sent his
Messenge r to translate them to that All-Perfec t, Glorious, and Celestial
Lodge above, and today they labor where the Supreme Grand Master of
the universe forever presides.
Death is an inescapable experience. "The almighty fiat has gone
forth, 'Dust thou art and unto dust shalt thou return,' and that we are all
subject to that decree, the daily observation of our lives furnishes evidence
not to be forgotten. " We pause in our deliberations and rejoicing to pay
our last tribute of respect and affection to the memory of our brethren who
have left us during the past year.
Since our last Annual Communication three hundred twenty-on e of
our members, Past Masters of their lodges, have reached the end of their
earthly toil. Two hundred thirty-two of our lodges suffered losses. One
hundred sixty-thre e lodges lost one Past Master each: fifty-four lodges
lost two: eleven 'lodges lost three: three lodges, Alhambra No. 322, Las
Palmas No. 366, and Euclid No. 519, lost four; and California No. 1 lost
five of its Past Masters.
This is the first time in a number of years that we do not have to report
the death of a Past Grand Master, or a Grand Lodge Officer. Among
those who have passed, however, are Ira Danford Wheeler, a member of
the Homes Endowme nt Board: Clarence A. Trowbrid ge, former Inspector
and Senior Grand Steward in 1950: and David Whitelaw Tulloch, formerly member of Grand Lodge History Committee.

DAVID WHITELAW TULLOCH
Death came suddenly to David Whitelaw Tulloch on April 24, 1958,
in his seventy-ei ghth year. The day before his death he had served as
pall bearer at the funeral of a long-time friend. A member of a pioneer
family. he was born on August 18, 1880. His father was a pioneer
developer of water distribution, electric power, and milling, and his son
followed in his steps. The ruins of their mill still stand by the covered
bridge in Knights Ferry.
Brother Dave, as he was known, was raised in Summit Lodge No.
112. on March 7, 1903, and served as Master of this lodge for two years,
in 1921 and 1922. He became one of its most distinguished Past Masters.
He served this Grand Lodge on its History Committee.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNI A

Active in civic affairs, he served his district in the State Assembly in
the second decade of the century. Devoted to his church, he was active
in its many activities throughou t the years.
His sudden passing came as a distinct shock to his many friends,
and this Grand Lodge Jost another faithful member.

~as a bulwark of the congregat ion to which he belonged. He served
his community, having at different times been a member of his City
Council and District Schoo] Board. For over sixty years of adult life
i~ his commu?ity he had stood for that which was just and right. Sometimes men differed with his opinions but all recognized his integrity.
Santa Clara was better because Carl Wesley Haman lived there.
_Not many of the departed were privileged to serve for as long a
period. Not all were endowed with equal talents, but we like to think
the consecration of our brother was typical of all who have passed on.
In lodges from the Oregon line to the Mexican border, and from the
sea to the great mountains, they served Masonry, their God, and their
fellow men up to the measure of their strength in the time permitted them
here on earth. Today as we meet in this beautiful new Temple we
honor thei.r :111emory and thank God that they were our brethren. They
are not pnvileged to be here but they labored, and their labors have not
been in vain.

CLARENCE A. TROWBRID GE

Brother Clarence A . Trowbrid ge passed away in Quincy, California,
on July 5, 1958.
A member of Semper Virens Lodge No. 552, he served that lodge ·
as its Master in 1947. He was the Grand Senior Steward of the Grand
Lodge in 1950. On the formation of Masonic District No. 300, Brother
Trowbrid ge was appointed Inspector, serving with honor and distinction until he was transferre d by his company from Arcata to Quincy in
1957. At the time of his death he was district representa tive for Pacific
Gas and Electric Company at Quincy, and had been associated with that
company for many years. He was active in the Pacific Service Employees Association.
During his residence in the Arcata area he was High. Priest of Humboldt Chapter No. 52, Royal Arch Masons. He was a member of
Pacific Council, Royal and Select Masters, and of Camelia Chapter:
Order of Eastern Star. He was an active member of Eureka Speakers
Club and of the First Christian Church, Eureka.
Brother Trowbrid ge is survived by his wife, who resides in Quincy,
and a married daughter, to whom our sympathy goes out.
One of his dose associates in Arcata writes, "Brother Trowbrid ge
was a fine man and Mason, well liked by all who knew him, and I personally consider it a privilege to have called him my friend and brother."
A complete list of all who have passed away is appended to, and
will be published as a part of this report. Although many are worthy of
special mention, in the time at our disposal it is impossible even to call
the full roll, much less give special mention to all who merit it. As we
read over the list, none of us will know all, or perhaps many of the names,
but each one will find one or two or more names which have real significance-th e names of Brothers we have known and loved. What manner
of men were these brethren who are no longer with us? The writer found
the name of a brother he had known for over thirty years. When we first
met he was a Past Master and Treasurer of his lodge, and continued to
serve as Treasurer over the intervening years. At the time of his death he
had been a Mason for just over sixty-five years. We do not know how
often he attended Grand Lodge and he probably never served as a
Grand Lodge Officer or Committeeman, but over all the years he was
constant in his attendanc e at his own lodge, and the wisdom of his
councils was always respectful ly considered. His handshak e was one of
the pleasures of visiting his lodge. A loyal member of his church, he

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON LODGE FINANCING
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Financing takes pleasure
in presenting to you its annual report of activities during the year of
1958.
The past year has been a rewarding one to the members of the
Committee on Lodge Financing through the excellent cooperation
of the constituent lodges of the Jurisdiction. When called upon, every
lodge and temple association has joined in a concerted effort to show
their willingness to cooperate even though at times it caused considerable sacrifice of time and effort on their part to adjust financial
conditions of their respective temple associations to conform to Masonic law. It has not been all sweetness and light, but all the problems
that arose were adjusted in the true spirit of Masonic brotherhood and
fraternal relations. There cannot be sufficient space to set forth all
the specific instances of progress, so a general report will be here
given. We of the Committee on Lodge Financing are pleased to report
to you in this portion of its report of some of the general work it has
done in the past year to correct the matters which were reported in
the last Grand Lodge Communication concerning the losses sustained
by temple associations in California.

GRAND LODGE OP CALIPORNIA

233

During the past year members of this committee made 132 visitations to lodges and temple associations to counsel with them concerning problems of incorporation, building, securing sites for future building, sales of real estate and adjustment of financial structures and rental
income in order to conform to the provisions of Section 409 of the
Masonic Code. Five exceedingly troublesome situations have been
equitably adjusted and many temple associations have made slight
adjustments that have considerably enhanced their financial structure.
Specifically, of 228 financial and profit and loss statements of an equal
number of temple associations. 136 of them now show a profit Only
92 show losses in varying amounts. The amount of profit shown by
the 136 temple associations amounted to $245,583.00, while those which
comprised the 92 which showed a loss only lost a total of $82,101.00.
Taking all the reporting temple associations into consideration, we
arrive at a net income over expenses of $163,482.00. Based upon a valuation of the assets of the total of 228 temple associations that reported
during 1958 of $14,190,179.00 the percentage represented by the profit
of $163,482.00 reflects a more healthy financial condition than that of
prior years.
While the figures set forth in the preceding paragraph represent
an increasingly healthy financial condition of Masonic Temple Associations, there is yet much room for improvement. We of the committee
feel that until ALL the temple associations in our Jurisdiction can
show a proper depreciation reserve and still have income which is
greater than expenses we can not truthfully consider ourselves out of
the woods. We do feel, however, that with the continued efforts of
the Masons in ~alifornia, and the excellent spirit of cooperation that
was evidence during the past year, the day will not be far off when we
all can say with pride that we are now financially sound.
We of the committee wish to extend our personal regards and
heart-felt thanks to the officers and members of Grand Lodge who
have encouraged and assisted us when such was needed.
To all the Masons in California we can say that your contributions
and efforts in the building of Masonic Temples and the outstanding success you have achieved is proof that when Masons work together in
the true spirit of Masonry, they can even accomplish the impossible.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Your committee investigated with the aid of Inspector J. Wesley
Sibole. learned that the plot belonged to old St. Mark's Lodge No. 85 of
Fiddletown. The charter of this lodge was revoked in 1894. No record
of this cemetery was found in the office of our Grand Secretary. A quick
search of the title revealed that on February 8. 1871. a deed to lots 26
and 27 of Block 11 Fiddletown was delivered to St. Mark's Lodge No.
85. This deed was never recorded in the Amador County records. However, the County Recorder informed us that the title is still good as it
was a Judges certificate. The property is located in the northe~st comer
of the community cemetery. not separately fenced, and contains .63 of
an acre.
It would appear from Sections 384 and 413 of the California Masonic
Code that, "other property of every kind" should have included the
cemetery. On the other hand, the tru~!ee appo~~ed ~y Gr~nd Lodge
may have felt that it would hardly be most Jud1c10us to dispose of a
cemetery.
So that this item may be cleared for the record and proper title established, your Committee on Cemeteries recommends:
1. That a proper title search be authorized and that the necessary
funds be allocated for this purpose.
2. That should the title prove that Lots 26 and 27 of Block 11,
Fiddletown. still remain in the name of St. Mark's Lodge No. 85, that
the ownership thereof be transferred to the Grand Lodge of California.
3. That should this property come into the hands of the Grand Lodge
of California through lawful transfer of ownership, that Grand Lodge
take immediate steps to restore that portion of the Community Cemetery
now owned by Grand Lodge and that it be made an historical monument
to our brothers of St. Mark's Lodge No. 85 and to the ghost town of
Fiddletown.
4. That should the above recommendations be accepted, that arrangements for its perpetual care be set up by Grand Lodge.
5. That should it be the will of Grand Lodge that they accept these
recommendations, then sufficient funds should be allocated to accomplish
this memorial.
RECOMMENDAT ION No. 2
IN REGARD TO SECTION 200 CALIFORNIA MASONIC CODE
Section 200 of the California Masonic Code says that all Masonic
Lodges owning and operating real property .•. shall submit an annual
profit-and-loss statement to the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge
Financing.
Your Committee on Cemeteries believes that it was not the intent
of Grand Lodge in the enactment of Section 200 to include our Masonic
cemeteries. Nevertheless. as we read this section, we can see no other
interpretation than that they are included. A lodge owning a Masonic
cemetery is certainly "owning and operating real property."
We. therefore, recommend:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

253

1. That all -lodges owning Masonic cemeteries, including those
owned jointly with other lodges or other organizations, be informed that
they come within the full scope of Section 200 of the California Masonic
Code.
2. That they be required under Section 200 of the California Masonic
Code to 6.le a profit-and-loss statement at the close of each fiscal year
of such lodge. cemetery association or corporation, with the Grand Lodge
Committee on Lodge Financing.
RECOMMENDAT ION No. 3
IN REGARD TO SECTION 199. CALIFORNIA MASONIC CODE

Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries feels that for so many
years we have been ~nclined to ignore our cemeteries, that when such
legislation as Section 199 of the California Masonic Code is written or
interpreted, we are inclined to forget our cemetery problem. We therefore, suggest and recommend that Section 199 be amended by the
addition of a new sub-section so as to specifically include cemeteries.
Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries recommends:
1. That a new sub-section be added to Section 199 of the California
Masonic Code, to be known as sub-section 4.
2. That this sub-section be so worded as to specifically cover the
formation of a Masonic Cemetery by a Masonic lodge or lodges.
RECOMMENDAT ION No. 4
ANNUAL CEMETERY REPORT FROM LoDGES

Your Committee on Masonic Cemeteries has found many plots
neglected or in disuse. It is our studied opinion that many of the places
in which our dead lie buried are no longer suitable due to the continued
neglect and lack of interest of the lodge membership.
In 1891, M. ·.w.·.Past Grand Master Alvan R. Conklin ruled, "that
the providing of a suitable place for burial of its dead, and the maintenance thereof. are legitimate expenses of a lodge."
It is the opinion of the committee that an annual report from those
lodges owning cemeteries should serve as a continual reminder of their
.
obligation.
Your Cemetery Committee, therefore, recommends:
1. That all lodges owning Masonic cemeteries or any part of such
cemeteries be required to submit an annual report to the Grand ·L odge
Committee on Cemeteries.
2. That such report shall show in detail the name of the lodge, the
name of the cemetery, its corporate name, date of organization, size of
property, number of lots sold, number remaining unsold, number of lots
sold during current fiscal year, amount expended for maintenance during
current fiscal year, condition of cemetery, and a copy of their profit-andloss statement.
3. That each lodge owning any portion of a Masonic cemetery main-
